Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. Additionally, we introduce an improved version of our algorithm with an additional $O(K\log{K})$ factor, potentially leading to significant practical applications. Furthermore, we use the variational Bayes approach to analyze the K-means prior and posterior distributions and, by adapting a Gaussian representation, develop a quantum version of this Bayesian framework resulting in the Q-EM algorithm. This algorithm, based on the EM algorithm, achieves an impressive speedup with an additional $O(K^{1/2}(N/P)^{3/2})$ factor, potentially leading to significant practical applications. These findings represent a significant step towards applying quantum computing to machine learning. A comprehensive, open-source code to reproduce these results is provided at https://github.com/quantummachinelearning/qml_research/tree/main/kmeans_qml.

In other words, it can only control pitch so much.  We suggest two new algorithms to fix this issue.  First, we came up with a pitch-shifting technique that doesn't change a speaker's unique voice characteristics, which helps make new speech samples sound more natural.  We also developed a training technique where FastPitch is taught to recognize speech with a range of pitches all for the same sentence.  Experimental results show that these algorithms help make FastPitch easier to control.  By using the first method, we found about a 10 dB improvement in how natural the speech sounds, and about a 5 dB improvement when using the second method.  Combining both techniques gives an extra 2 dB improvement.  We also found that using the first method lets FastPitch's quality stay the same even when teaching it a wide range of pitches, which is a big deal. Our study investigates lepton pair production in proton-proton collisions, specifically neutral-current Drell-Yan processes, incorporating the effects of bottom-quark fragmentation for the first time within the NNLO QCD framework. The analysis considers up-to-date PDF sets and accounts for the impact of both CSPPZ and MMPK PDFs on the underlying calculation. The results demonstrate a noticeable discrepancy between including or omitting the effects of b-quark fragmentation, estimated to be approximately 10% of the total cross-section at 14 TeV and 33% at 27 TeV, primarily driven by the contribution of large-transverse-momentum b-quarks. Given the significance of this effect and its potential to affect measurements of the abelian coupling constant, we recommend that future studies prioritize a more precise understanding of the b-quark contribution during data analysis. Additionally, the analysis highlights the importance of a detailed treatment of fragmentation functions to accurately describe non-perturbative aspects of low-energy observables. This research addresses the challenge of clustering high-dimensional data, which differs from traditional clustering in its use of varied feature importance. We propose a novel method, called Weighted K-means (WK-means), to handle this issue, allowing for dynamic feature weighting without assuming equal importance. The proposed approach adapts to changing feature weights by introducing a representation matrix to transform the original features into a new, optimized space. The formulation integrates both weighted clustering and non-linear dimensionality reduction. Theoretical justification is provided for the algorithm, which is shown to be consistent under certain conditions. Empirical evidence, derived from synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method in achieving better results compared to existing alternatives. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become a crucial component of many machine learning applications, particularly in natural language processing, computer vision, and reinforcement learning. However, existing algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle with local optima issues, particularly when the model expert dimensions differ. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative algorithm based on the Proximal U-Grad (PUG) method, which incorporates a form of variational regularization. This approach, known as Proximal U-Gaussian (PUGS), relies on the Univariate Gaussian distribution for expert weighting and regularization. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that PUGS is guaranteed to converge to a stable stationary point under regular Lipschitz conditions. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that PUGS achieves superior performance in both synthetic and real-world applications, such as MoE-based neural machine translation. This research offers an innovative solution for training MoE models and serves as a foundation for exploring other distribution-based weighting methods. The implementation details are available on GitHub at https://github.com/quantum-q/pung. Moreover, the source of the moe-based neural machine translation dataset can be found on the DBLP website.

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to help a deep neural network (DNN) use its previous training on multiple areas to successfully learn new skills without extensive, labor-intensive fine-tuning. In recent years, pre-trained models such as BERT have greatly improved the efficiency of NLP processes. Even very small adjustments to the pre-trained model and their training objectives can significantly decrease how well a model adapts to new tasks. Researchers have previously proposed methods, such as edge weight modification and minimum connection, to improve the ability of DNNs to adapt to new tasks. However, these models still rely on a single source of pre-training. In this study, a new method called level-based weight modification is proposed to improve the ability of DNNs to adapt to new tasks. This method considers the different levels of importance within a multi-task pre-trained model and modifies the weights of the final fully connected layers based on this hierarchy. We also conducted an extensive analysis of how different factors, such as modifying model weights and adjusting training objectives, affect the ability of DNNs to adapt to new tasks. Our study further improves the understanding of NML and LBM by comparing them with other competing methods, such as MC and EDW. We evaluated the proposed LBM method on a variety of benchmark datasets and found it to be more effective than other competing methods. Our study also provided new insights into the state-of-the-art techniques and factors that contribute to the ability of DNNs to adapt to new tasks. The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, where malicious actors modify APK files directly to evade detection. The study aims to explore this type of attack that often receives insufficient attention due to a lack of knowledge about the Android ecosystem or a focus on general evasion attacks. The study will examine the characteristics of problem-space evasion attacks, typically associated with a small number of samples, close relationships, and sequential modifications within the same app package space. To confirm this analysis, the study will investigate the properties of problem-space evasion samples using statistical methods and provide recommendations for creating effective detection systems that adapt to the specific challenges of problem-space evasion attacks. The analysis will also discuss the potential consequences of these attacks on Android users and the necessary improvements in detection systems and security best practices to better resist this type of threat. The study will conclude with a comprehensive overview of problem-space evasion attacks and discuss promising areas for future research. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 defines problem-space evasion attacks, Section 3 discusses their types, Section 4 examines past studies, Section 5 investigates the characteristics of problem-space evasion samples, and Section 6 provides future directions and concludes the study. The final section includes an assessment of the severity of problem-space evasion attacks, a summary of findings, and suggestions for developers to enhance the security of their Android apps. The last section discusses future research directions and concludes the study. The study is conducted under the following assumptions: (1) problem-space evasion attacks occur through direct modifications to APK files, (2) the goal of these attacks is to evade malware detection systems, and (3) the focus is on users' security risks, detection systems, and best practices. The learning problem in neural networks has been re-examined using a Boolean circuit model. A Boolean circuit is composed of gates that output Boolean values and is equivalent to a circuit consisting of Boolean functions. We investigated the minimum number of gates required for a Boolean circuit to solve a given learning task using the VC dimension concept, which led to an upper limit of $n\log n$ gates needed to learn a dataset of $n$ examples. However, this estimate held under certain restrictions: the dataset must be i.i.d. and drawn from a uniform distribution; the dataset must not include the target function; and the dataset must not contain functions with a negative correlation to the target function. When these conditions were not met, significantly more gates were required. Specifically, if a dataset follows a uniform correlation distribution, then the minimum number of gates required to learn it increases to the number of elements in the set, even for simple tasks. These findings shed new light on the requirements for neural networks to learn given data and show that current neural networks, which often require millions of parameters, may be insufficient to learn certain tasks, highlighting the need for an even greater number of parameters. Notably, this need is not merely an increase in parameters, as adding them randomly would not solve the problem; rather, a more nuanced increase in parameters, possibly through a more sophisticated distribution, is required to learn the data. These findings suggest that the design of deep learning models should be reevaluated. A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, which can automatically identify key patterns in the data. The Deep InfoMax (DIM) method, in particular, utilizes a supervised approach by maximizing the representation's mutual information with both the input and a target image. This paper presents a modified version of DIM, called DIM-S, that instead captures the similarity between the representation and a set of predefined, high-quality representations. This substitution allows DIM-S to operate without the need for target images, making it more practical for use in studies involving humans, as it raises privacy concerns to utilize target images. The paper demonstrates that DIM-S can successfully preserve the original representation, and validates its effectiveness through a series of experiments on semi-synthetic and real datasets, particularly focusing on semi-supervised Alzheimer's disease diagnosis. Compared to other approaches, DIM-S-SiC is shown to achieve a high performance of 84.6% with only 102 training samples. Additionally, the modified model, DIM-S-Multi, is used to generate a comprehensive proteomic brain atlas, which is then applied to a potential clinical application - diagnosing multiple sclerosis based on brain MRI images, and yields a competitive performance of 77.5% compared to other approaches. This research showcases the versatility of DIM-S in enhancing task performance, and highlights its potential as a reliable method for brain disease diagnosis. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zyliu92/DIM-S. Furthermore, the generated proteomic brain atlas can be accessed at https://www.cmu.edu/hcml/proteomic-brain-atlas/proteomic-brain-atlas.html. Lastly, the derived multiple sclerosis diagnosis model can be integrated into a web-based platform for medical professionals to utilize in real-world applications, and can be accessed at https://cmu-hcml-dim-s-multi-ms.github.io/ms-diagnosis.html. A metastable dark matter candidate emerges as a natural consequence of a
conformal transformation between Einstein's gravity and a higher-dimensional loveland theory.
This process yields a short-range interaction between dark matter particles at low velocities.
The weak equivalence principle holds strictly in this framework, which implies that dark matter
behavior will be similar to baryons at low speeds. The application of this principle allows us
to distinguish the loveland model from other theories, such as long-range Yukawa interactions.
The loveland model produces a dark matter candidate that survives until today only if its mass
is greater than approximately one trillion GeV, given the current understanding of the universe's age.
The likelihood of decaying dark matter particles with long lifetimes, a feature of the loveland model,
offers a new explanation for the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry. The loveland model's
dark matter particles can be in a state of "frozen quantum chaos" and may emit unusual, quantum
sounds at extremely low frequencies. The potential for detecting these particles and sounds at
future, high-energy dark matter experiments is explored. The study also examines the possibility of
related dark matter signatures in cosmic microwave background data and future, high-resolution
spectroscopic surveys. The loveland model's implications for the stability of nuclear fusions and
possible particle-like features in dark matter are also examined. The analysis reveals that the
loveland model's short-range interaction and metastable dark matter candidate have significant
consequences for the universe's early and late phases. The universe's early phases show signs of
particle-like behavior, while its late phases show signs of quantum inactivity in dark matter.

This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and limitations. To achieve this, a Boltzmann machine architecture is employed as a reference model. Within this study, it is discovered that incremental Hebbian learning can produce and amplify complex patterns in a system. A comprehensive examination of this learning rule's properties is conducted, and it is concluded that it satisfies the essential requirements for generating and maintaining complex systems. On the other hand, global symmetry and non-linearity, two key features found in some theoretical models, do not play a crucial role in generating complexity. Consequently, it is suggested that these models focus primarily on preserving stability, not complexity. Furthermore, it is found that the widely-used Mackey-Glass time series predictor, which associates non-linearity with symmetry, actually fails to achieve long-term stability without incorporating additional non-linearity. This failure highlights the significance of distinguishing between necessity and sufficiency in developing effective time series prediction algorithms. A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the ability to accomplish the process even when the system Hamiltonian is unknown. This is because these protocols utilize an essential element called the instantaneous driving term, which can be calculated from the desired flux and quantum state, regardless of the Hamiltonian. This research focuses on the limitations of this instantaneous driving term, defining the 'gray zones' where these protocols are ineffective due to insufficient data in the driving basis. This concept is illustrated through the analysis of two established systems, where the initial investigation is the quantum harmonic oscillator and the subsequent study is the Jaynes-Cummings system. In both cases, the structure of the gray zones is determined. This study demonstrates that 'gray zones' may not always be narrow and that they may have intricate structures, and it raises important questions about the applicability and limitations of counterdiabatic protocols in various situations. Furthermore, this research highlights a crucial point: the availability of a useful instantaneous driving term does not automatically make a counterdiabatic protocol effective, and a thorough analysis of the system is necessary to achieve a desired state change. Additionally, this research offers a new and important criterion for evaluating the usefulness of counterdiabatic protocols, which is the requirement that the system must be able to access the target state through at least one instantaneous driving term. If this criterion is not met, it indicates a fundamental limitation of these protocols, which can be essential for understanding their capabilities and limitations. This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series is derived for functions in $C^\infty$, which converges to the original function under specified conditions on the remainder term. Subsequent applications of these results enable the computation of certain infinite series connected to Stirling numbers. Moreover, the paper addresses the differentiation of infinite series, provides an alternative representation of differentiable functions, and extends the application of these findings to complex-valued probability distributions. Additionally, the paper investigates the uniqueness of the differentiable representation and differentiates complex-valued discrete distributions. Lastly, the paper examines the differentiability of the Riemann zeta function and its analogues, facilitated by the application of the exponents method. Specifically, it finds the first and second derivatives of the zeta function, and the derivatives of the alternating zeta function, as well as expressing higher-order derivatives of the zeta function as the sum of exponentials. Furthermore, the paper computes Stirling numbers of the second kind for various values of $n$ and $k$. Lastly, the paper presents a characterization of differentiable logarithmic derivatives of the Riemann zeta function, in terms of holomorphic functions, and identifies a candidate for the third derivative of the zeta function. Lastly, it identifies potential research directions, as outlined in the concluding section. Several of the findings presented in this study have been validated numerically. Infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions of several variables and complex-valued functions on compact sets in multi-dimensional spaces are also explored in the accompanying studies. Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to the pair (S, d) results in a branched covering. Consequently, if (S, d) is topologically equivalent to the two-dimensional sphere S^2, it then becomes conformally equivalent to S^2. This condition is necessary for almost conformal harmonic maps to exist. This study also explores its implications on the study of surfaces with bounded curvature, particularly in a novel framework that encompasses those with constant curvature. Furthermore, it resolves a long-standing conjecture of F. Lehecka and D. Weiss, addressing a question originally posed by M. G. Park and D. Weiss. Additionally, it offers a new proof that can be applied to prove the Franke-Warren conjecture. Lastly, through established relationships, it provides a novel interpretation of Thurston's Paskalina Conjecture. The study relies heavily on integration of techniques from Riemannian geometry, differential geometry, and the theory of branched coverings. It also delves into the challenge of extending its findings to higher dimensions. Finally, through established connections, it provides a novel reinterpretation of the conjecture of Riemann. It's been established that this problem aligns with functional dependencies and first-order identities. In this paper, we focus on the typed IRI constructor aspect, proposing a schema-constrained solution based on certain typed IRI constructors. To achieve this, we develop a novel language that combines features of first-order identities and the typed IRI constructor, resulting in the creation of a language hierarchy with the previously studied $\mathcal{C}^{+}$ from Buneman et al. (2001). Additionally, we show that the problem of validating instances against this language is tractable, with an algorithm we develop for data validation having a linear runtime complexity in relation to data size. We further investigate this problem by generalizing it to the case with subject-less quadruple assertions, containing an additional dimension of type compatibility between corresponding resources, revealing a corresponding language hierarchy with the previously studied $\mathcal{C}$ from Fagin et al. (2005). In this generalized scenario, we show that the problem of validating instances against this quadruple language is also tractable, with an algorithm we develop for data validation having a linear runtime complexity in relation to data size. We conclude that the problem of RDF data exchange involving subject-less triple and quadruple assertions is tractable in the context of typed IRI constructors. Based on these findings, we propose an algorithm for data exchange, resulting in an algorithm hierarchy with previously studied solutions from Bueter et al. (2011) and Fagin et al. (2009). Finally, we show that the problem of subject-based RDF data exchange according to Bueter et al. (2011) is a specific instance of the generalized problem studied here for quadruple assertions. A practical implementation of our algorithm for subject-based RDF data exchange is provided in the Bueter et al. (2015) case study. This study proposes an innovative mass reconstruction technique for producing scalar bosons of low mass at the LHC, specifically utilizing the $ZZ \to 4\ell$ process in conjunction with the CLIC four momentum reconstruction algorithm. By utilizing the $2 \to 2$ scattering matrix formulation, we have developed a novel method for calculating the differential production cross-section, leveraging the distribution of reconstructed, center-of-mass energy for $ZZ$ pairs. With the assistance of sophisticated neural networks, such as a Gaussian process, we have established a regression tool that enables the conversion of the reconstructed, center-of-mass energy distribution to a mass reconstruction spectrum that accurately reflects the underlying physics. Using simulated CLIC data, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of this new method, which significantly improves the mass resolution by a factor of $\sim\sqrt{10}$ compared to the CLIC's four momentum reconstruction algorithm while maintaining an equivalent level of systematic uncertainty. Furthermore, we have examined the new method's resilience against various systematic uncertainties, such as trigger bias, beam halo, and quantum effects like beam stripping, finding that it performs satisfactorily even in the presence of these potential issues. Additionally, we have also successfully applied this novel method to the $Z\gamma$ process, which produces a mass resolution nearly an order of magnitude better than the four momentum reconstruction algorithm. Overall, we have found that this proposed method significantly enhances the new physics sensitivity at CLIC by a factor of $\sim\sqrt{5}$ compared to the current state-of-the-art technique. With further optimization and refinement, we anticipate that this new method will significantly improve the mass resolution, ultimately making it a highly effective tool for particle physics research. The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through 73 VFTS spectra analyses it has been observed that Be-type stars have higher rotational speeds. Calculations reveal that their estimated mean rotational speed of 250km/s is significantly higher than their B-type counterparts and roughly half the speed of O-type stars. Furthermore, these Be-type stars have their faster rotational rates confined to their outer regions which could be a result of their dual star evolution. Additionally, chemical abundance analyses have revealed that their lighter elements are distributed uniformly, whereas their heavier elements are concentrated towards their outer regions. It has been hypothesised that this distribution could be a result of a massive accretion event occurring from a companion star that eventually collapsed into a black hole or neutron star. With the expectation that this scenario should lead to a dual wind pattern, it has been observed that this dual pattern is only evident in the hotter elements like helium and ionized nitrogen, whereas the cooler elements like iron are still emitted from the Be-type star in a single spherical pattern. errors. In contrast, we suggest a weakly-supervised anagram transformation learning
approach that directly copies ASR errors, including errors in punctuation, word order
and word choice. This method is inspired by the voluntary errors in spoken language.

ASR output with high error rates, and we also develop an extended AnCIL model using
constrained adversarial learning. Our findings demonstrate that small batches of
spoken language anagrams can effectively teach ITN systems without the need for written
text corrections. Furthermore, our proposed AnCIL model outperforms a strong
baseline by a significant margin, setting the stage for future advancements in this
area. All the code and data required to reproduce our results are publicly available

In line with this, studies have discovered a connection between residual entropy and viscosity in molecular fluids. This being the case, we examine the entropy and shear viscosity in simple fluids comprised of soft spheres through the lens of the soft-sphere fluid model. This model offers a high level of flexibility, allowing for variable softness in the spheres, which in turn greatly impacts the entropy of the fluid. In order to accurately model the shear viscosity of the fluid, we develop a theoretical model grounded in the approach of Mori, which takes into account the correlation between shear viscosity and residual entropy. Our findings demonstrate that, with a single parameter adjustment, which accounts for the degree of softness in the spheres, our model accurately reproduces the entropy and shear viscosity of the fluid across their respective temperature profiles. In addition, our model was found to have a robust mathematical structure that is well-suited for complex modeling purposes. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the intricate relationship between the short-range, attractive, and repulsive interactions in the fluid, which is well-represented by the soft-sphere fluid model. This model has the advantage of being significantly simpler than other molecular fluid models, which makes it a valuable tool for understanding and predicting the thermodynamic and hydrodynamic properties of fluids. In order to verify our model, we compared the entropy and shear viscosity of the fluid as modeled by the soft-sphere fluid approach to corresponding results obtained through molecular dynamics simulations. Our findings demonstrate a strong, quantitative agreement between our model and the simulation data. In particular, our model was found to have a high level of accuracy, even for the early time frames that are typically challenging to model. In addition, our analysis highlights the simplicity and versatility of the soft-sphere fluid approach, which offers a valuable tool for understanding and predicting the thermodynamic and hydrodynamic properties of fluids. In particular, our model was found to have the potential to greatly reduce the computational resources required for molecular dynamics simulations, which could lead to significant practical applications and benefits. The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic cycle of expansion, which alternates between matter domination and dark energy domination, is explored. This periodic behavior is proposed as an alternative to the theoretical Lambda Cold Dark Matter model. If the dark energy equivalent to the vacuum energy of quantum field theory, coupled with very weak interactions, constitutes most of the dark energy, then the matter density would likely decrease to a low value before the next matter-dominated era, causing the cycle to be disrupted. It is suggested that the first cycle of this periodic cosmology is already in progress, with the matter density decreasing toward the next cycle. The proposed cosmology likely violates the standard model of particle physics's energy conservation principle due to the large difference between the vacuum energy and the total dark energy. This discrepancy could be resolved if the standard model's matter and energy, which would constitute a small fraction of the total, would not contribute to the dark energy. This idea is compared to the theory of the cosmological constant, which would maintain the conservation of the standard model's energy during the periods of dark energy domination. However, the proposed periodic cosmology likely avoids the theoretical issues associated with the dark energy problem. This paper explores the theoretical and observational implications of the proposed periodic cosmology, starting with the theoretical issues, and then analyzing the observations that contradict this theory. The theoretical issues discussed include the theoretical issues of the matter cycle's disruption, the conservation of the standard model's energy during the periods of dark energy domination, the theoretical issues of the matter cycle's disruption, the deuterium problem, and the discrepancy between the ages of the oldest stars and the cosmic frame. However, the proposed periodic cosmology is consistent with the observations of the galaxy, which suggest that the matter density is insufficient to cause the matter cycle's disruption before the observation period. This discrepancy between the observations of the cosmic microwave background radiation and the galaxy, and the proposed periodic cosmology, is likely due to the proposed periodic cosmology being an intermediate state between the matter-dominated cycle and the dark energy-dominated cycle. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NNs that can recognize keywords with minimal computational effort. We create a new, efficient Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture that requires less power to run continuously on devices. Our CNN design achieves an impressive balance of accuracy and low energy consumption, making it suitable for always-on keyword recognition. We test and compare the performance of our CNN with existing NN models on datasets from popular speech datasets. Our results show that this new CNN architecture outperforms existing NN models in terms of accuracy and energy efficiency, even when powered only intermittently. We study the relationship between model size and energy consumption in NNs. Our findings indicate that models with fewer parameters tend to be more energy-efficient. Our NN models are trained using a binary classification scheme to recognize keywords with a silicon-based neural engine. However, this engine is not compatible with our training process, so we transfer the weights of our models to a compatible format for testing on this kernel. Our test reveals that the new CNN architecture performs better than other NN models in terms of accuracy and energy efficiency. To confirm the practical application of our model, we compare its performance with a commercial smart speaker kernel. Our results show that the new CNN architecture reaches 98% of the commercial model's accuracy with only 2% of the commercial model's parameters. Our test also shows that the new CNN architecture consumes 7.5 to 13 times less energy to run continuously on devices. However, the energy-saving effect is more pronounced with the binary NN model. We conclude that the new CNN architecture is a suitable choice for always-on keyword recognition. We believe this model can be improved by adding more complex features to it. Our work lays the groundwork for the application of CNNs to keyword spotting. We believe this architecture has the potential to be applied to other speech-related tasks. We are studying complex scaling as an inherent property unique to complex number systems and its applications. By extending the complex domain without considering complex scaling, deep learning models miss an inherent complex advantage. To fill this gap, we propose the Complex Scaling Unit (CSU) to incorporate complex scaling into neural networks, where the CSU's performance far surpasses the conventional real-value unit. Several complex applications, such as image and data compression, speech analysis and synthesis, and molecular prediction, have been explored with the CSU. The experiments reveal the CSU's capability in achieving better performance on both predictive tasks and lossless data compression, while its application in the spectrogram domain yields state-of-the-art results in speech analysis and synthesis. Furthermore, the CSU's application in molecular prediction yields performance comparable to the current top-level methods. Through analytical means, we demonstrate the CSU's ability to achieve state-of-the-art results without resorting to numerous neural network training epochs. Ultimately, we find that complex scaling has extensive value and can be effectively leveraged by incorporating the CSU into real-valued deep learning models. The code used in this study is publicly available at https://github.com/ComplexAI/Complex_Scaling_Unit.

Researchers utilize quantum simulations to investigate complex many-body systems by replicating their underlying Hamiltonians. However, the challenge of accessing certain system properties through accessible initial states necessitates the use of unitary transformations to produce these states from the base states. A specific set of transformations involving single-excitation states is often employed, but a proposed alternative uses qubit-excitation evolutions instead. Theoretical assessments indicate the potential for significant cost reductions in computational requirements when these evolutions are applied in simulations. A corresponding proof-of-principle experiment has been performed on a quantum processor to compare the efficacy of qubit-excitation evolutions with fermionic-excitation evolutions. When qubit-excitation evolutions were used, a $40$ times reduction in computational requirements was achieved, with a significant improvement in sampling efficiency of up to $10^5$. This breakthrough paves the way for the development of novel algorithms tailored to the capabilities of quantum processors with restricted qubit connectivity. A related code to support these experiments can be accessed via the provided link to the GitHub repository. Additionally, the specifications of the custom quantum processor used in the study are outlined in the supplementary information section. A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of representation, likelihood, and prior in an unsupervised setting. Typically, a variational autoencoder (VAE) and its modifications prioritize maximizing the ELBO and approximating posterior distributions in order to achieve a reasonable trade-off between compression and prediction. However, optimizing these models can be challenging due to the requirement for Monte Carlo sampling in both encoder and decoder networks, which significantly hampers training speed. Furthermore, the variational approach can result in suboptimal solutions due to the approximated posterior distribution and the trade-off between compression and prediction. We propose a new framework, the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), which removes the sampling step from both the encoder and decoder. Instead, we use a normalizing flow to transform a continuous Gaussian distribution into a discrete distribution for classification. By eliminating sampling, the DGD's optimization process is greatly simplified and its training speed greatly increased. Thanks to the power of normalizing flows, the DGD is able to learn a more accurate representation of the data, avoiding the limitations of the variational approach. By integrating a variational approach to inference only, the DGD's generative sampling step is further alleviated, allowing the model to prioritize the trade-off between compression and prediction based on its own performance. We test the DGD on multiple datasets, including unsupervised image rotation, visual representation learning, and data compression, demonstrating its ability to produce competitive results with both state-of-the-art VAEs and GANs, as well as its potential as a powerful generative model in its own right. Code is available at https://github.com/ghassenhammami/Deep-Generative-Decoder. As an additional contribution, we release the first open-source platform for unsupervised image and object pose calculation, called image-object-poses (IOP), which integrates the DGD at its core. IOP allows users to easily train an unsupervised image representation using the DGD, calculate object pose from a single image, and integrate the model with popular 3D engines for easy visualization. This platform has the potential to greatly accelerate research in this area by providing a simple interface for both researchers and practitioners to work with. A detailed tutorial is available to guide users in training the DGD and utilizing the IOP platform. By providing the IOP platform, we aim to accelerate research in this area by providing an easy-to-use interface that simplifies training the DGD and calculating object pose. We successfully observed several volatile molecules including H$_2$O, CO, HCO, HCN, and H$_2$O$_2$ in the comet's inner atmosphere. By analyzing these emissions, we derived the spatially integrated column densities of these molecules, along with their production and destruction rates, and compared them with the findings from other comets that made close approaches to the Sun (with a distance of 1.5 astronomical units or less). Our research also involved estimating the relative abundances of these molecules in the comet by using its water abundance as a reference. It was observed that the emissions from H$_2$O, CO, and HCN were of type I, indicating that they were produced through the processes of gas-phase chemistry, while the H$_2$O$_2$ emissions were of type I-II, suggesting additional sources of production. The HCO emissions were of type I-IId, indicating that they were primarily produced through the interaction between the solar wind and the comet's highly energized atoms and molecules. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Moreover, the unsupervised approach enables novel speech categories to be discovered and modeled. Building on the core innovation of a conditional variational autoencoder, our method consists of three primary components: (1) a neural network-generated speech prior, (2) a neural transducer that maps the prior to spoken words and prosody, including a dictionary-based posterior, and (3) a post-processing neural network. We have successfully tested the unsupervised system on the Google Speech Dataset and the Librispeech dataset, which contained no overlap with the training data. This research represents the first achievement of unsupervised high-quality speech synthesis. All of the code and models used in this study have been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ouou1125/USpeechSyn. We hope that this study will open up new avenues in the exploration of unsupervised methods for speech synthesis. For each case study, a Pareto front is provided along with a single-best solution obtained through multi-criteria mixed-integer non-linear programming. A plan for the project's future expansion is also presented, including the potential for regional networks to be established and integrated into the Dynaswap structure. Ultimately, this paper seeks to establish Dynaswap as a pioneering initiative that will pave the way for a global, interconnected cyberinfrastructure security system. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect of an item, such as a restaurant or a product. However, existing studies have an inherent issue: they rarely consider the significance of words in the context of the task. Recent findings have revealed that ignoring word importance can lead to lower accuracy in aspect-based sentiment analysis. This study introduces a novel data set from the IMDB movie reviews, which takes into account the contribution of each word in the reviews, categorizing the sentiment as overall or part-specific (implicit). We also present a model that utilizes the unique characteristics of aspect-based sentiment analysis, incorporating a word importance factor. The model's performance is compared with the current best models in the field, and the experimental results show that it achieves high accuracy when the word importance is known. Furthermore, our study introduces a new challenge that focuses on predicting the word importance, and the accompanying data set is accessible at: https://github.com/zhengwang2018/ABSAnet. The data set can also be obtained by emailing the principal author. Through detailed error analysis, we discovered that the model performs poorly in the overall sentiment classification due to the difficulty in capturing overall sentiment words, and it struggles to determine part-specific sentiment when there is a lack of relevant context for the specific aspect. The proposed model demonstrates the importance of word importance in aspect-based sentiment analysis, and it offers a new perspective on this task. The model's code and data are publicly available on GitHub at: https://github.com/zhengwang2018/ABSAnet. By incorporating temperature and chemical potential, thermal Yang-Mills-aether theory is formulated and examined through the vacuum graph representation and heat kernel expansion, focusing on thermodynamic properties and a key characteristic function. A key outcome of this analysis is the determination that non-abelian aether terms cause a variation in the relationship between thermodynamic properties and central charge, thereby altering the relationship between temperature and central charge. A key aspect of our work involves addressing potential concerns regarding time dilation and Lorentzian anomalies in the context of non-relativistic quantum field theory, emphasizing that non-abelian aether terms violate time dilation and generate Lorentzian anomalies even at relativistic velocities. This instability can lead to a significant ejection of mass, a process that is observed in total quasar surveys. This study investigates the mass ejection phenomenon in mergers of spinning black holes, focusing on their final state stability. We used numerical simulations, including black hole perturbations and merger calculations with high-order schemes, to analyze mass ejection. Our findings show that there is a strong relationship between the final black hole's spin and the amount of ejected mass, with higher spins corresponding to greater ejection. This is consistent with earlier findings using a different approach. However, when the mass ejection is compared to a specific parameter, a critical angle that describes the tilt of the accretion disk, a strong correlation emerges. This correlation could provide valuable insights into the growth of massive black holes through the merger of intermediate-mass black holes. This process may be supported by the observation of a specific binary quasar. Additionally, a new method to estimate the spin of black holes using data from total quasar surveys has been developed. This technique leverages the mass ejection observed in these surveys and the correlation between the spin and ejected mass. By combining these correlations with mass and spin constraints from a specific parameterization of accretion, a distribution of black hole spins in total quasar surveys can be generated. This technique is used to fit the data from two specific surveys, resulting in constraints on the mean and spin distribution of black hole spins. We analyzed a subset of 1058,800 galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program, which spans ~$8500$ deg$^2$ and consists of galaxies with masses above $10^{10}$ M$_\odot$. Our sample is drawn from two catalogs with overlapping fields, and we estimate that our findings are representative of galaxies without strong redshift biases. Approximately 30% of these massive galaxies exhibit notable tidal development, characterized by a luminosity exceeding 1% within a radius of $0.25$ half-light radii. Moreover, we observed that tidal development often occurs in conjunction with other markers of galaxy interactions. Although the data do not allow us to discern the temporal sequence of events, we found that tidal development can accompany a range of markers of galaxy interactions across multiple combinations. Interestingly, the frequency of tidal development does not appear to be influenced by galactic environment. A significant portion of tidal development without accompanying brightness fluctuations suggests that tidal development can occur without preceding mergers. Furthermore, we observed that tidal development is more common in galaxies with higher rotation speeds and lower brightness fluctuations. If our galaxies serve as a proxy for the population of tidal development markers at higher masses, our findings have significant implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution. Based on the rate of tidal development, it appears that a given galaxy will undergo three or more encounters with another galaxy within its first 4 billion years. Consequently, the extent to which tidal development is correlated with brightness fluctuations may be reduced over time. However, the data do not allow us to discern the temporal sequence of events. Therefore, the question of whether tidal development always precedes brightness fluctuations remains an open one. Furthermore, the extent to which tidal development is more common in galaxies with higher rotation speeds may be due to tidal development serving as a trigger for the transfer of angular momentum. However, the data do not allow us to discern the direction of causality. Therefore, the question of whether tidal development can serve as a trigger for the transfer of angular momentum, thereby increasing rotation speed, remains an open one. This paper is a continuation of my study on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a theory that offers an alternative to the classical Laplace equation in modeling gravitational fields. The premise of the ASTG is supported by numerous pieces of evidence suggesting repulsive gravitational forces in the polar regions of massive objects. A key advantage of the ASTG is that it generates potential energy solutions that are infinitely smooth and have a natural singularity-free boundary, eliminating the need for a gravitational "cut-off." The paper begins by examining a basic, straightforward example of a circularly symmetric mass distribution and proceeds to analyze a more complex case, a two-dimensional mass distribution shaped like the letter 'D'. It shows that the ASTG can be effectively used to solve a wide range of mass distributions by combining multiple basic, fundamental cases. The paper also touches on the potential applications of the ASTG to astrophysical phenomena, noting that it may provide a valuable framework for exploring phenomena that are typically difficult to model with the classical Laplace equation. A notable example is the spiral density waves observed in certain galaxies, which are thought to be the result of gravitational interactions between mass distributions. The ASTG is shown to generate potential energy solutions that exhibit smooth, continuous spiral patterns, suggesting that the theory may offer insights into the underlying mechanisms driving such phenomena. The paper concludes by highlighting the potential implications of the ASTG from a fundamental, world-view perspective, suggesting that the observation of smooth, continuous gravitational fields could have profound implications for our understanding of space-time and its behavior. As an alternative to the classical Newton-Laplace model, the ASTG is presented as a thought-provoking framework that can help us better comprehend the complexities of gravitational interactions and the beauty of classical gravitational theory. The paper concludes by offering a final, speculative note on the potential connections between the ASTG and modern quantum gravity theories. It is proposed that the ASTG may provide a valuable framework for exploring relationships between classical and quantum gravity, potentially shedding light on the mysteries of space-time and its behavior. The paper concludes with a final, thought-provoking question, inviting the reader to consider the potential implications of observed repulsive gravitational effects and their potential to revolutionize our understanding of classical gravitational theory and its relationship with quantum gravity. We have gathered a vast dataset of observations during and following fast radio bursts, making it the largest compilation to date. Our findings from optical monitoring of seven FRBs reveal no discernible optical bursts beyond the initial 5-second window following the burst. The lack of optical emission was well within the expected bounds for most pulsars. Their most stringent limit, at a level of $10^{41}$ erg s$^{-67}$, was established for the pulsar PSR B0740-25. The theoretical model of radiation powered pulsars, based on pulsar characteristics such as those of PSR J0319-1848, predicts flare energies in excess of $10^{48}$ erg. Therefore, in order to reconcile this discrepancy, a significant portion of energy must be released after the initial 5-second window, or there must be significant variation in the efficiency of radiation power among the population. Theoretical radiative efficiency should also be reevaluated. We observed two FRBs at later times and found their flux levels to be within expected limits. One of the bursts exhibited a moderate afterglow lasting several minutes. Our detailed analysis suggests that its afterglow may be attributed to the scattering of diffused optical radiation from surrounding intergalactic medium. A similar afterglow was not detected in the other burst. We performed a comprehensive examination of the coalescing binary merger afterglow, identified a limitation in the available data, and determined that the afterglow emission in the optical spectrum is likely to be weak. Nevertheless, in the pursuit of improved understanding, we recommend the implementation of targeted, multi-messenger follow-ups of FRBs originating from local galaxies. Such studies offer a unique opportunity to study the coalescing binary merger afterglow, potentially yielding valuable insights into the underlying physics. Two supplementary papers offer additional information on the following topics: a detailed description of afterglow simulations in the case of FRB 2020-319, and a discussion on soft X-ray and optical spectral behaviors in the 16 October 2020 FRB population. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called QNOG, which drives the optimization of quantized neural networks that produce qualitily-robust explanations. Quantization is a widely used method to reduce model size through limited weight and activation precision. However, this process typically leads to overquantization in layers dealing with sensory data, hindering the accuracy of deep learning models. To address this challenge, we frame the quantization stage as a multi-objective optimization problem, aiming to optimize the quality and robustness of the model. Furthermore, we propose a novel optimization algorithm called QNOG, which incorporates quality and robustness gradients during optimization, achieving superior results compared to the state-of-the-art methods in quantized neural networks. Our approach accelerates the optimization process by approximating quantization operation and treating robust gradient computation as a layer. This enables efficient gradient computation and application of gradient-based optimization algorithms. When applied to the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets, QNOG significantly outperforms existing methods in quality and robustness, with remarkable improvements of 2.64% and 4.34%, respectively. Additionally, our method achieves better results on the Tiny ImageNet dataset, producing a remarkable gain of 2.35% in quality and 4.65% in robustness. The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robots that more closely resemble the anatomy of invertebrate creatures and flexible human tissues. To introduce the concepts and challenges of this innovative research area, we will be teaching a survey course that explores the fundamental theories and practical obstacles of this technology. Since continuum robots have a high degree of intrinsic instability due to their continuous and deformable structure, controlling and modeling their movements can be very complex. This study provides an overview of the significant advancements in designing algorithms and computational models for continuum robots, as well as the various control difficulties associated with dynamic manipulation and the use of sensory inputs. Additionally, it discusses the potential benefits and initial applications of this technology, highlighting its relevance to fields like medical robotics, where the manipulation of delicate tissues is required. To make this information more accessible, we have structured this review into four primary sections, focusing on the control problems faced by continuum robots, the advancements in algorithms and modeling, the integration of sensory inputs, and the perspectives on future applications. This comprehensive survey aims to provide an understanding of the theoretical foundations and practical difficulties of this modern robotics field, offering an up-to-date review of the state-of-the-art research and representing a valuable resource for professionals working with continuum robots. This course is intended for students who have a basic understanding of robotics and mechatronics, as well as those interested in the field, including researchers, professionals, and anyone curious about the state-of-the-art research and potential applications of continuum soft robots. To facilitate easy comprehension, a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/rafael-sasaki/Continuum-Soft-Robotics) has been established with all the review's content and supplementary materials embedded in a digital environment. This repository includes 3D models and videos demonstrating the mechanics and movement simulations of continuum robots, as well as a list of recommended articles and research papers and a list of the main actors in this innovative robotics field. This review is part of a series of educational resources, including video lectures, which will be made available on YouTube and described in more detail within the review. This digital environment is intended to provide a space for interactions and discussions among the community, where readers can share their thoughts and engage with the topic, providing valuable contributions to the research area. This review is a unique opportunity to explore the potential benefits and initial applications of continuum soft robots and is an invitation to the community to participate in this fascinating and innovative robotics field. The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however, current advancements are primarily based on supervised methods, which benefit from greater control and higher visual quality. Despite this, the challenge of generating images of multiple classes remains, largely due to the difficulty in developing effective supervisory signals and optimizing models for diverse tasks. Our contribution to this area is GASSP-GAN, a novel generative adversarial network designed to learn the distribution of diverse classes simultaneously. The approach leverages one-hot supervisory signals and modifies the loss function to accommodate multiple classification tasks. The GASSP-GAN model also introduces a novel feature that allows it to specialize different generators for various tasks while sharing a single encoder and a dual discriminator network. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on multiple classification tasks, including one-way and two-way classifications in various datasets. The findings reveal that our approach achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art single-task models while significantly outperforming multi-task models in terms of visual quality and diversity. To make the maximum-likelihood estimation method more versatile for real-world use in particle physics experiments detecting rare events, we need to address its significant computational bottleneck. The Markov Chain Monte Carlo method is able to overcome this limitation, but choosing the right algorithm can be tricky. We found that differential evolution algorithms are well-suited for high-dimensional problems and reliable in practice, outperforming other options. In this context, we introduce DEs as variations of the maximum-likelihood estimation algorithm and outline the modifications needed to make them work efficiently by sampling from a posterior probability distribution. We then propose an efficient way to sample from this distribution by breaking it down into simpler subsets and using a series of conditional probability calculations. To validate the proposed model, a case study was conducted to demonstrate its performance using a dataset collected from an offshore wind turbine. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/N_\varphi^c$ possesses the property $R_\infty$, where $N_\varphi^c$ denotes the normal closure of $\varphi^c(G)$ in G. In this paper, we obtain the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of generalised solvable metabelian groups. Specifically, for a pair of prime numbers p and q, we define $G_{p,q}$ as the group $\langle a, b, c | [a, b] = 1, [a, c] = c, [c, b] = a^p, [c, a] = a^q \rangle$, and investigate the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of $G_{p,q}$ for various values of p and q. We establish that a metabelian group G has property $R_\infty$ if and only if its maximal normal $R_\infty$-nilpotent derived subgroup divides the commutator height of the center of G, and use this criterion to examine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of $G_{p,q}$ for odd prime p. We show that a nilpotent degree of 5 is achievable for even prime p and unachievable for prime p = 2. This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from instrumented vehicles in South-Central England. Distinct from existing driving datasets like DAVE02 and DART, SceNDD features instrumented vehicle data combined with driver-centric scene descriptions, enabling a comprehensive understanding of the road environment. Our primary objective is to facilitate the development of autonomous driving applications utilizing an end-to-end approach, requiring detailed scene representations and driver views. As a pioneering dataset collection efforts reveal, the description of driving scenes varies significantly among individual drivers, necessitating datasets like SceNDD that capture the diversity of driving contexts. SceNDD features over 4000 scene descriptions, each detailing approximately 20 objects, as well as corresponding driver views, road network data, and instrumented vehicle data, including sensor readings and vehicle telemetry. Our research demonstrates the application of SceNDD in training end-to-end driving models by integrating it with existing naturalistic driving datasets, DAVE02 and DART. Our findings indicate that incorporating SceNDD leads to a notable improvement in object detection accuracy, increasing the number of objects detected by 13% compared to an end-to-end model trained on a single dataset. We are investigating a type of equality related to the work exerted on a system being observed with unsharp, non-projective measurement methods. These methods have no clear outcomes, and they blur the boundary between the system before the measurement and the measuring device itself. To handle this situation, we introduce a up-to-date commutator-based approach to determine the performance of energy measurements, which relies on the resolution of the measuring device to assess their quality. This approach aligns with the principles of standard quantum measurement practices. We examine the commutator method in the context of a harmonic oscillator model. Using this approach, we establish a work equal to, or less than, the energy of the system divided by 2 times the square root of the average resolution, multiplied by a prefactor based on the entropy of the system before the measurement. For comparison purposes, we also investigate the work equal to, or less than, the energy of the system divided by 2 times the standard deviation of the Hamiltonian, as proposed by Theunissen et al. This alternative approach is applicable when the entropy of the system is negligible, and it yields a work equal to, or less than, the energy of the system divided by 2 times the standard deviation of the Hamiltonian, multiplied by a prefactor that depends on the correlation between the Hamiltonian and its square. We demonstrate that, in the case of a Coherent state, the commutator method yields a work equal to, or less than, the energy of the system divided by 2 times the square root of the average resolution, which approaches the energy of the system divided by 2 times the standard deviation of the Hamiltonian for high resolution or high energy. This research reveals the complexity of unsharp measurement methods and the need to consider their performance in the context of thermodynamics. It also sheds light on the limitations of projective measurement practices and the importance of understanding the quality of measurement methods before drawing conclusions about the performance of thermodynamic processes. To illustrate the applicability of the commutator method, we examine the case of a quantum harmonic oscillator that undergoes unidirectional collision with an unsharp detector, which may be a meter with finite resolution or an infinitely fine probe that blurs the boundary between the system before the measurement and the measuring device itself. This research paves the way for the development of new thermodynamic protocols for unsharp measurement methods, which will be explored in depth in a companion paper. Furthermore, the commutator method reveals the importance of thermodynamic uncertainty principles

This paper provides a comprehensive, two-dimensional study of how $J/\psi$ is produced in ultra-peripheral collisions using LHCb data collected from 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV. Specifically, the research focuses on di-lepton di-muon final states that result from $J/\psi$ decay. The analysis is divided into two parts, with the first examining how $J/\psi$ is polarized in collisions and how this polarization varies based on the rapidity and transverse momentum of the muons. This part of the analysis also compares the results to theoretical models such as Goulianos' model and to predictions from photon-photon and photon-nucleon calculations. In the second part of the analysis, the researchers study how $J/\psi$ is polarized in collisions and compare this to $\chi_{c0}$ decays, with the results also being compared to theoretical models and to predictions of photon-photon and photon-nucleon calculations. However, in both cases, the experimental results do not agree with the predictions of the Goulianos model. On the contrary, the results do fit well with the predictions of other models such as Goulianos' model being ruled out. Furthermore, the research discovered that $J/\psi$ produced in collisions is predominantly polarized in a state of even angular momentum and positive parity. This research is significant as it provides the first measurement of how $J/\psi$ is polarized in collisions and sets a new standard for understanding this process. Additionally, the research discovered that when $J/\psi$ is produced in collisions, it has a rapidity distribution that is centered around mid-rapidity and a similar transverse momentum distribution as $\chi_{c0}$ decays. This research is important as it provides new insights into the physics of how $J/\psi$ is produced in collisions and how this process can be used to better understand the physics. This research is further significant as it provides new insights into the properties of exotic particles that may be discovered in future research. Numerous languages attribute gender to inanimate objects, resulting in words representing different types of entities across genders. This characteristic, known as grammatical gender, has a considerable impact on words' semantic representations. In this study, we investigate and assess the influence of grammatical gender on the word embeddings created through neural networks. Our investigation focuses on Hebrew, a Semitic language featuring four genders, to examine the capacity of current word embedding models to capture this grammatical distinction. Our analysis indicates that these models are capable of learning the gender-related meanings of words, with the result that words of the same gender exhibit greater semantic similarity compared to words of differing genders. Furthermore, our discoveries suggest that reducing the model's capacity to capture context at the sentence level can enhance the ability of the model to distinguish between words of varying genders. Our model was trained using the Israeli Hebrew dataset HEIT, comprising 7 million word-context pairs. Our results were validated through a human-based evaluation, revealing a meaningful distinction in the semantic similarity of words belonging to the same versus different genders. By applying human annotations, we demonstrated that these learned representations can be utilized to identify a word's gender with considerable accuracy. Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual object recognition systems, 
despite significant challenges in predicting the orientation for novel object categories.
Recent top-performing methods primarily rely on large pre-existing datasets for training.
This study proposes an end-to-end object recognition system capable of predicting object orientations 
from novel object categories solely based on a single image without any prior training.
Results show that the proposed method achieves impressive performance on several benchmarks. 
For instance, it accurately predicts object orientations with over 70% accuracy for both yaw and pitch 
angles on the XBlock dataset, surpassing state-of-the-art performance by nearly 30%. 
This method's key innovation lies in using a rotation-aware loss function during training. 
This loss function predicts object orientations by measuring the angular distance between predicted 
object orientations and the predicted 3D object shape based on a Convolutional Neural Network. 
Instead of directly predicting the object orientation, the network predicts the 3D shape, which the network 
then uses to calculate the object orientation.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data requires efficient processing to achieve accurate radio signal reconstruction. Current processing techniques, primarily used for traditional single-polarization data, become cumbersome when handling the expanded data rates of modern interferometers. This study develops and evaluates novel hardware-based methods to process the expanded data of the LOFAR telescope, which operates with four polarizations and generates high data rates. We design and prototype two reconfigurable hardware accelerators, one for each processing approach, and compare their performance with software-based processing. The results show that both hardware solutions significantly outperform their software counterparts by two orders of magnitude, while also reducing energy consumption by 10% to 30%. Furthermore, the hardware approaches demonstrate improved latency compared to software processing due to lower setup costs. Overall, the proposed hardware solutions effectively handle the high data rates of modern interferometers, such as LOFAR, and are scalable for future large-scale radio telescopes with increased polarizations and data rates. The developed accelerators are a crucial step towards building efficient big-data pipelines for the expanded data of the expanded LOFAR, which will enhance data analysis and reconstruction tasks. Additionally, this work paves the way for the application of machine learning algorithms on the accelerated data to improve signal-to-noise ratio and data quality. The hardware designs are open-source and open-hardware, contributing to the advancement of radio astronomy and data processing fields. Conventional methods, however, often rely on outdated and inefficient techniques. In recent years, a more effective approach using data-driven models has been explored. Despite its promise, model learning in this context poses significant challenges. First, frequency and voltage are non-linear variables. Second, voltage is heavily influenced by load and past conditions. To address these issues, we propose a novel deep learning technique that leverages a hybrid framework. Specifically, we use a hybrid model combining a frequency model and a voltage model. The frequency model relies on time-series data, while the voltage model uses both current and past voltage data. The results demonstrate the efficiency of our approach in learning models for frequency and voltage. In quantum betting scenarios, two players wager on the outcomes of measurements from a shared quantum system, often governed by rules such as the Majumdar-Rosen-Bush algorithm. This note reimagines their rules in a different context - betting. By viewing their game as a form of betting, we can examine its underpinning physical principles using the concepts of classical betting theory and ergotropy, a measure of a quantum system's energy potential. To better understand the rules of the Majumdar-Rosen-Bush game, we first apply a theorem from classical betting theory, known as Kelly's theorem, to determine the optimal betting strategies and their associated earnings. We then explore the ergotropy of the quantum outcomes, ultimately concluding that the Majumdar-Rosen-Bush game does not yield physically realizable strategies. By using ergotropy, we can also derive lower limits on the achievable betting gains, shedding new light on the physical laws governing the game. This approach enables us to identify two distinct cases, one in which the game adheres to realizable betting principles and another in which it does not, leading to the formulation of an open problem that may illuminate the Majumdar-Rosen-Bush game's properties. In a final section, we extend our analysis of the Majumdar-Rosen-Bush game to other quantum systems, including spinless particles and particles in three-dimensional space, as well as examining the game's realizability in these contexts. By viewing the Majumdar-Rosen-Bush game through the lens of ergotropy and betting theory, we have gained deeper insights into its underlying physical laws, sparking further discussion on this topic. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the potential utility of ergotropy in the field of quantum information and betting. The last section of this work presents an alternative strategy for the Bohmian quantum coin-tossing protocol, a simpler approach that does not require the entanglement of quantum systems. By using the ergotropy of the Bohmian quantum coin, we can derive a lower limit on the achievable betting gains, a finding that may hold practical significance in the implementation of this protocol. Lastly, the appendix of this work revisits the concept of ergotropy with regard to information and betting, identifying an apparent contradiction between its original definition by Aberg and a revised definition proposed in this work, a finding that may have significant implications for the field of quantum information and betting. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the target of interest, accumulate an additional systematic error related to the atmospheric dispersion position. Various correction methods have been developed for reducing this error but the development of such methods typically requires time-consuming and costly observations of calibration sources or stars with distinct spectral properties. To address this issue, a software-based approach was developed to estimate atmospheric dispersion corrections using a large amount of astronomical image data. Coupled with a neural network-based image simulation, the atmospheric dispersion correction models can be generated from a single image of a multiple-star system with multiple components having different spectral properties. This approach was successfully demonstrated on multiple-star systems of different spectral types and was used to calculate the ADCs needed for observing and analyzing multiple-star systems including HIP 14842, HIP 14843, and HIP 11816. The project's software tools were made available under a free and open-source license for public use and its results show that the developed method can effectively reduce the uncertainty in off-axis observations by a factor of ten or more. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies like Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global pandemic accelerated this shift, resulting in an unprecedented number of employees transitioning to fully remote work. Consequently, the issue of employee well-being in remote working has become a pressing concern. Existing research primarily focuses on productivity in remote working, yet there is a lack of comprehensive studies on well-being. This study aims to bridge this gap by examining the impact of Scrum implementation on remote working well-being. Employing a theory of human needs, we developed the Remote Working Well-being (RWW) scale to create a new measure. This scale, based on interviews and surveys with 289 employees, identifies two key factors that contribute to remote working well-being: Scrum implementation and individual personality traits. Our findings highlight the importance of two fundamental human needs, autonomy and competence, in remote working settings. Moreover, the study introduces a new concept - the social connection need - and shows that it can be fulfilled through Scrum's daily stand-up meetings. Finally, we discuss practical implications and suggest future research directions. This study offers valuable insights to practitioners on enhancing remote working well-being and provides a framework for improving practice. Ultimately, it is shown that Scrum can support three essential human needs, thereby creating a beneficial environment for remote workers' well-being. This research contributes to the field by identifying the specific well-being needs of remote workers and exploring ways to fulfill them. It is hoped that this research will inspire further studies on this topic. The study's findings have been shared with the Scrum Alliance community, influencing their practices and policies. The RWW scale has been registered with the US Patent office and is available for researchers to use in future studies. The study's code is openly accessible on GitHub, located at https://github.com/RemoteScrum/RemoteScrum. The research data can be found at https://github.com/WellbeingScale/WellbeingScale.
