By making a change of variables, the expression for the maximum achievable signal gain can be re-expressed as a function of the total transmitted power in the network and the number of users, and it converges to a specific value as the number of users approaches infinity. Additionally, this expression can be used to determine the maximum achievable signal gain for suboptimal power control strategies with a similar convergence behavior when the number of users approaches infinity. Several of these derived expressions are graphed to illustrate how the maximum achievable signal gain changes as a function of the total transmitted power in the network. Furthermore, the expression for the maximum achievable signal gain when using optimal power control is also graphed to show how it compares to the expressions derived for various suboptimal power control strategies. This comparison reveals that these suboptimal power control strategies can achieve a very large fraction of the maximum achievable signal gain when the number of users is very large. This implies that these suboptimal power control strategies can be very useful for large networks, and they are likely to be nearly as good as optimal power control when the number of users is very large. This work also introduces an expression for the entropy of the noise as a function of the total bandwidth in the network, which may be of independent interest due to its broader applicability. This study focuses on the potential of inter-atom entanglement to detect a quantum chemical reaction similarity index, utilizing a quantum version of the k-means clustering algorithm. We examine how inter-atom entanglement changes when transitioning from one chemical state to another in a molecule. Based on this approach, a quantum classifier is developed to determine whether a molecule in a specific state undergoes a chemical reaction similarity or difference. We evaluated the performance of our quantum classifier on hydrogen molecule $H_2$ and hydrogensodium $H\,Na$ molecules in a quantum version of the k-means clustering setting. The results demonstrate that the quantum classifier achieves high accuracy, comparable to a classical classifier based on classical neural networks. Accurate prediction of radio wave transmission is essential for ensuring reliable communication between terrestrial, aerial, and space-based devices. Various propagation models have been developed to forecast signal strength under diverse conditions, typically segregated into two sub-models - ground-based models and space-based models. The former encompasses models like the Hata-Crow model and the ITU-R model, which account for signal obstruction caused by the ground, whereas the latter includes models such as the Levanon model and the MIMO channel spatio-temporal correlation model, which consider inter-device signals. A combined model that efficiently integrates both categories has not been previously established. This work presents a novel radio propagation model that unifies ground-based and space-based models, leveraging the advantages of both and offering improved performance. The new model's effectiveness is validated by demonstrating that it accurately estimates and generalizes radio wave transmission under various conditions, particularly in situations not encountered during its training. This result indicates that the model can be safely deployed in new environments. Videos illustrating the model's capabilities are available at https://www.cedras.org/tvprop/db_video_db.html. A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm based on that semantics. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We also demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful. Specifically, we examine and fix unintended behavior in a well-known temporal planning verification algorithm, known as validation algorithm TLPlan as described in planning research by Artale et al. (2013). Our study indicates that the proposed semantics is particularly suitable for a high-level representation of temporal planning, enabling efficient automated verification of verification algorithms. We further Isabelle/HOL-proved that our validation algorithm is sound when applied to all planning tasks conforming to the defined semantics. Ultimately, these findings emphasize the value of formal methods in guaranteeing the correctness of verification algorithms for temporal planning. We make the Isabelle/HOL development with the proven validation algorithm available online through the Coq-Z3-Isabelle project. To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise categorization of individual documents is crucial. Currently, classification mainly relies on human expertise, but semi-supervised Machine Learning algorithms can aid this process by utilizing limited labeled data and estimating the distribution of the remaining unlabeled records. Despite their assistance, these ML algorithms still require a substantial amount of labeled input, which may be impractical to obtain. To mitigate this limitation, we propose an innovative system that leverages the structure of mathematical journals to automatically classify STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) documents. By recognizing the crucial role that mathematical entities play in journal organization, our approach aims to enhance the efficiency of STEM document classification. Unlike traditional methods, ours utilizes semantic information at the publication level to enhance classification accuracy. We tested our proposed classification method on a large collection of 85,921 STEM documents, covering multiple fields, and compared its performance to the standard random walk and flow-based classification methods, demonstrating its superiority in accuracy. By streamlining the classification process and reducing the need for extensive labeled data, our method can help streamline information organization and retrieval systems. As the need for precise document classification continues to grow with the rapid expansion of available digital information, our classification method is well-positioned to address this challenge. By applying our proposed classification method to the document collection of the OpenMath repository, we were able to accurately identify 1945 journal articles, providing valuable insights into how mathematical entities contribute to journal organization and informing our understanding of scholarly communication processes. By analyzing the mathematical entities that distinguish different journals, we were able to identify patterns in communication and data visualization opportunities. For example, the application of yourcata taxonomy on mathematical entities allowed us to identify the dominant mathematical entities that characterized individual journals, providing valuable insights into the structure of the mathematical discipline. By using these categorizations, we were able to accurately predict the journal subject codes that match the classification of the mathematical entities used within each publication. A significant assumption in these models is that each potential match has a complete and ordered list of potential partners, an assumption often violated in real scenarios. This study explores the stable matching algorithms when this condition is relaxed, resulting in which no single algorithm can guarantee optimal solutions in all cases. However, when agents' preference lists are limited to a manageable number of options, this study reveals a strategy to develop a unique stable matching solution under specific constraints. This result provides an advantage in settings where agents' preference lists are short yet their overall number remains significant. A practical application of this finding is a new algorithm to match students with schools when school lists are the primary consideration. This algorithm is particularly useful in scenarios with a large number of schools and a limited number of students, as it produces a stable match that would also satisfy an exact matching if one could be found. Additionally, the study introduces a novel concept called 'weak-AP match' that serves as a form of partial compensation in situations where the stable match cannot be found exactly. Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly reliant on labels and do not consider what humans find important in a
summary. We propose a new metric called SummScore that uses four key measures to
assess summary quality: 1) how clearly the main points are represented; 2) the
overall coherence and organization of the summary; 3) how well the summary
represents the original text; and 4) its conciseness. These dimensions are
measured by analyzing how well various extractive and generative models perform
these tasks. By weighting the individual scores, SummScore provides a more
informative assessment of summary quality that is less reliant on manual labeling.
We also compare SummScore to existing evaluation metrics and examine its
performance across various language pairs and summarization datasets. Our
results indicate that SummScore is more reliable than existing evaluation metrics
and can be improved by optimizing certain hyperparameters. Additionally, we
developed SummScore from a large-scale pre-annotation of human summaries, which
enables the model to identify key summary points and their corresponding
relevance to the original text. We also investigate methods for reducing the
requirement for human labeling in SummScore and propose an alternative
reweighting approach that promotes diversity in how pre-annotated summaries are
evaluated. Overall, our study provides a more nuanced understanding of what
humans value in a summary and suggests that a multi-faceted approach, which
combines both automated and human-based methods of evaluation, is necessary to
improve the performance of summary evaluation metrics. These resources and the
SummScore code are available online.

labeling, diversity of pre-annotations, summary quality measurement.

A new method for extracting a multi-dimensional signal from cross-correlation data is presented. This type of data represents relationships between various measurements taken from the same entity but in different forms. The proposed algorithm is based on several key assumptions: the signal has a simple, low-dimensional "structure"; only its cross-correlation information is available; and only the diagonal of this cross-correlation matrix is fully known, whereas the rest is incomplete. The problem is reformulated into a semidefinite program (SDP), a mathematical optimization technique. The solution is sensitive to noise in the data but incorporates a regularization term to filter out unwanted information, thus enhancing signal recovery. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on synthetic and real-world data, specifically, images of polystyrene spheres taken under different forms of neutron radiation. The results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods, yielding a more detailed three-dimensional model of the spheres. The technique is available as a Python package called "cross-corr" on GitHub. The paper draws inspiration from the work of S. J. Wigington et al., who published their results in the journal NeurIPS in 2017. The current research expands on their findings by addressing the extracted signal as a multi-dimensional entity. The work also expands on their use of convex optimization techniques to extract the signal when only the cross-correlation of the signal is partially known. The results show that the proposed algorithm achieves high levels of signal recovery when the noise is present while outperforming existing methods. The conventional approach to 3D object detection, which relies on LiDAR data, is often limited by the scanning range of 100 meters due to the persistence encoding method used in most popular detectors, resulting in a significant 80% drop in accuracy beyond that range. This issue is exacerbated by the fact that this detection method provides incomplete and distorted information for objects outside the detection range. In response, we present 3D Det, a novel camera-based system for 3D object detection. By leveraging the near-infrared (NIR) channel in cameras, this system is able to operate effectively in bright environments and provide more accurate 3D bounding box geometry for objects within its visual field. Furthermore, we propose the Selective Encoder Network (SEN), which effectively processes persistence data by prioritizing information near the detection range, thereby improving LiDAR-based 3D object detectors by as much as 16% and 27% respectively in terms of average mAP. Experiments using our encoder have shown superior performance when combined with other popular detectors, resulting in substantial gains of up to 11% and 20% in average mAP. Notably, 3D Det outperforms state-of-the-art LiDAR-based detectors in cases where objects are located outside the detection range, with mAP increases of up to 14% and 26%. Finally, by combining camera and LiDAR data, we present Fusion Det, which uses SEN to process LiDAR data and provide more accurate 3D object detection by as much as 6% in average mAP. This result outperforms state-of-the-art multi-modal detectors in cases where camera and LiDAR data have overlapping fields of view, with mAP increases of up to 6% and 12%. We are investigating thermal variations in the scale of Kolmogorov $l_k$ for incompressible fluid turbulence, which is far beyond the reach of present supercomputers. To achieve this, a highly efficient simulation technique based on wavelet packets is used, taking advantage of the flexibility of tensor product formats to represent filtered equations in a highly parallelized manner. The resulting simulations are then combined using a convolution kernel to obtain statistical data up to a high level of filtering, from which we can draw inferences about the underlying physical process at the scale of $l_k$. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a mechanism to copy elements directly from questions. We put this enhanced architecture to the test using state-of-the-art datasets containing questions that involve novel knowledge elements. Compared to their standard counterparts, our results indicate substantial improvements across all datasets. With its exceptional performance, this approach has great potential to revolutionize automated SPARQL query generation. Its scalability and ease of use make it an ideal choice for researchers and practitioners. Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in multi-dimensional formats by leveraging low-rank properties. This is particularly significant in visual data recovery applications such as 4D texture completion from missing pixels or video reconstruction from damaged segments. Existing low-rank tensor completion methods, however, are often limited by high computational requirements and a lack of robustness against noise and outliers. This paper proposes a computational efficient and robust solution to tensor completion by formulating it as a convex optimization problem in the Bregman iteration framework. By utilizing a novel regularization term inspired by the "weighted median" matrix, we can incorporate the ability to resist the influence of noisy data and highlight the underlying patterns through median filtering across the data's matrix-wise structure. Additionally, we have developed a versatile and efficient algorithm based on Bregman iterations with a specific approach to updating the tensor data. This method can be applied to a wide range of data types and is well-suited for addressing 4D texture completion and multi-frame video reconstruction problems. Our proposed approach, as demonstrated by both simulated and real-world experiments, can effectively remove noise and recover missing data by robustly highlighting the underlying patterns in the data. Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, when instructed to predict tasks not seen during training, they demonstrate impressive performance using only task-specific prompting strategies. To optimize this zero-shot capability, we introduce the "meta-tuning" technique, which fine-tunes pre-trained language model parameters to parameterize task-specific prompting strategies. By doing so, we establish a robust framework for zero-shot learning that outperforms current best practices. Through experiments, we assess the relative effectiveness of fine-tuning model parameters versus fine-tuning prompting texts and highlight the substantial gains achievable through meta-tuning. Notably, our results indicate that meta-tuning yields better generalization than few-shot learning on comparable datasets, significantly broadening the applicability of pre-trained language models in zero-shot settings. This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to study the dynamics of the JQO model, an effective Heisenberg model with next-to-nearest neighbor interactions. The JQO model is particularly relevant for understanding the superfluid-to-magnetic phase transition in antiferromagnetic spin systems with 120-degree ordering. To simulate its dynamics, we go beyond previous work in the JQO model by investigating the response of the order parameter at low temperatures through the absorption of sound waves. The results confirm the existence of three distinct regimes: a normal fluid, a quasi-long range ordered state, and a magnetically ordered state. While the parameters that demarcate these regimes are consistent with prior static calculations, a more accurate approximation of the matrix product operators' time-evolution is necessary to study this model. To achieve this, we utilize a graph-based decomposition of the Hamiltonian that is well-suited for handling the JQO model's specific structure. This method allows for the efficient simulation of large systems, as it reduces the memory requirements associated with storing matrix product operators. To quantify the memory usage, we have optimized the algorithm for archiving these operators and have tested our approach on a variety of systems, specifically those used to study the spin-1 Heisenberg model on a triangular lattice. Our findings demonstrate that the graph-based decomposition of the Hamiltonian allows for the efficient simulation of large systems, resulting in the significant reduction of the computational time required to reach the final state. A corresponding decrease is observed in the memory requirements needed to compute the matrix product operators at any point in time. This development is particularly valuable for large systems, as it results in the substantial reduction of the computational time required to compute the momentum-space spin structure factor. The results of these simulations accurately capture the finite-size effects that arise from the quantum critical behavior of the JQO model. In particular, the graph-based decomposition of the Hamiltonian allows for the accurate computation of the momentum-space spin structure factor at low temperatures, resulting in the correct capture of the quantum critical behavior observed at the superfluid-to-magnetic phase transition. By analyzing various lattice configurations with different values of $L_t$, the researchers found that the phase transition depends heavily on this additional lattice element. Furthermore, adding random $Z_3$-invariant noise to the gauge action causes the phase transition to occur at high mass values when $L_t \ge 4$. A new kinetic model, the $\varphi$-SHS model, is presented for simulating rarefied monatomic gas flows. This model expands the SHS model to incorporate a scalar collision frequency, $\varphi$, which allows for the closure of the gain term in the generalized Boltzmann equation through a first-order approximation. This leads to the $\varphi$-SHS model being applicable for a wide range of monatomic gas collision rates, from very fast to very slow. An analytical evaluation of the SHS model's first-order approximation is carried out, which confirms its suitability for non-isothermal flow applications while producing minor errors in non-equilibrium flow simulations. A critical analysis of the $\varphi$-SHS model is performed using rigorous mathematical methods, which demonstrates that certain its key characteristics, such as its positivity and consistency, depend on the magnitude of the collision frequency. A comprehensive series of numerical simulations are performed to assess the $\varphi$-SHS model's performance. These simulations, which involve various monatomic gas test cases with diverse collision rates and complex flow conditions, show that the $\varphi$-SHS model produces highly accurate results, both in terms of flow field accuracy and overall efficiency. Furthermore, it is observed that the $\varphi$-SHS model's accuracy and efficiency are largely unaffected by the specific value of the collision frequency. This robustness is due, in part, to the $\varphi$-SHS model's ability to produce precise non-equilibrium Maxwellian representations, which serve as robust approximations in a wide range of monatomic gas applications. Overall, the $\varphi$-SHS model is shown to be a versatile and efficient kinetic modeling tool for a broad range of monatomic gas collision rates. This model has the potential to improve the simulation speed and accuracy of rarefied monatomic gas flow applications while producing highly accurate macroscopic flow predictions. Furthermore, the $\varphi$-SHS model's analytical evaluation provides valuable insights into the SHS model's behavior and can serve as a framework for future research into the development of collision frequency-dependent kinetic modeling tools. In the future, the $\varphi$-SHS model can be adapted for use in the simulation of rarefied polyatomic gas flows by incorporating additional complexity, such as the accommodation coefficients and additional degrees of freedom. Current state-of-the-art semantic parsers, however, fall short in tackling out-of-vocabulary request queries, which are particularly crucial for voice assistants to handle effectively in order to deliver seamless user experiences. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a novel semantic parsing algorithm grounded in pre-trained language models, which demonstrates impressive results in accuracy for out-of-vocabulary queries and also offers enhanced scalability in handling semantic parsing tasks. We further investigate the mechanisms through which the proposed algorithm achieves semantic parsing, utilizing visualizations and numerical metrics such as syntactic attention and token-level accuracy to illustrate its performance mechanisms. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm achieves greater efficiency in terms of processing speed by leveraging pre-trained models, which is substantiated by experiments and benchmark comparisons. Overall, the theoretical foundations, empirical assessments, and computational benefits suggest that the proposed parsing algorithm could potentially replace traditional parsing methods in real-world voice assistant applications. We validate the practical applicability of the proposed algorithm in dialogue-based scenarios through a Google Assistant-based case study, which showcases its outstanding performance in handling complex out-of-vocabulary queries in real-world settings. Using ALMA's H30α (231.90 GHz) observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we estimate the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) based on measured gas excitation and beam uncertainties. These observations, taken over a 30-second interval, revealed 127 identified H30α sources, of which 46 were matched to 25 known infrared sources and 81 were considered unassociated with visible counterparts. This led to the calculation of an unbiased SFR, as determined by the cumulative SFR from sources of all sizes, with a total SFR of 0.017 Msun/yr. Compared to the galaxy's integrated infrared SFR, this value represents approximately 18% of the total. Analyzing the resolved SFR with and without beam uncertainty, we found that the galaxy's SFR is primarily influenced by the galaxy's central disk. This resulted in the identification of SFR values ranging from 0.01 to 0.5 Msun/yr for individual sources, with a median value of 0.04 Msun/yr. Furthermore, the combined SFR value of sources associated with green pea-like objects was calculated as 0.06 Msun/yr, with a ratio of 0.33, indicating that these objects contribute less to the galaxy's SFR. Utilizing the known ionizing photon luminosity of these green pea-like objects, we determined a photoionization feedback efficiency of 3.6% for the galaxy NGC 5253. This value is consistent with that of the galaxy NGC 1569, however, the galaxy NGC 5253 displays reduced SFR density and star formation efficiency. This may be attributed to the galaxy NGC 5253 being in a less active star burst phase. This study also found that the galaxy NGC 5253 has a reduced SFR efficiency compared to the galaxy NGC 1569 and the galaxy Mrk 1275, however the galaxy NGC 5253 shows SFR efficiency similar to that of the galaxy IC 10. Potential reasons for the galaxy NGC 5253's reduced SFR efficiency could be the presence of a super massive black hole or the interaction with a nearby galaxy. This study also found that the galaxy NGC 5253 has a reduced SFR efficiency for green pea-like objects when compared to the galaxy IC 10. Potential reasons for the galaxy NGC 5253's reduced SFR efficiency could be the presence of a super massive black hole or the interaction with a nearby galaxy.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain domain under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and develop a Hilbert--Schmidt operator approximation that yields a quantifiable error bound as an $L^2(X)$ norm. This approximation can be used to create nonparametric confidence intervals and hypothesis tests based on $H_0: \rho(X,Y) = 0$ versus $H_1: \rho(X,Y) \neq 0$, where $\rho$ represents the correlation between $X$ and $Y$. We illustrate the utility of our operator through a numerical example. Furthermore, we discuss how our findings can be used to estimate the $L^2$-norm of a nonparametric estimator for the conditional mean based on a kernel estimate of the conditional density of $Y$ given $X$. This work is accepted in Annals of Statistics, Vol. 48, No. 4, 2020.

By utilizing a 3D photonic band gap crystal made from silicon, an optimized light-absorbing layer can be achieved with enhanced total absorption within the wavelength range of 600-1100 nm. Two photonic band gap crystal structures, consisting of low-doped silicon with carbon and oxygen, were generated using atomic-scale relaxation and energy-minimizing processes. These crystal structures exhibit a robust band gap spanning the visible and near-infrared spectral regions. Calculations of absorption for photons reflected back through the cell reveal that a photonic band gap crystal can boost total absorption by 5% compared to a metal back reflector, with even greater gains of up to 13% for infrared photons. Nevertheless, a photonic band gap crystal may disrupt charge transport in the cell, potentially leading to decreased efficiency due to increased light scattering and increased bulk recombination. An alternative design involving a photonic band gap crystal integrated within a light-trapping structure is proposed to mitigate these negative effects, and the resulting structure is shown to improve the solar cell efficiency by 4%. This improved design features an anti-refective coating, a photonic band gap crystal, and an irregular nanostructure front surface, all working together to increase the light-trapped area through increased scattering and enhanced absorption, particularly in the front surface of the cell. These findings indicate that photonic band gap crystals offer a promising option for enhancing thin-film silicon solar cells with both improved absorption capabilities and integrated charge carrier management. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging, thereby offering superior performance and reduced error rates compared to current methods. Although DL-based image fusion methods have been widely studied, they have yet to be rigorously evaluated in the context of fire imagery, and to date, no comprehensive dataset has been made available that features visible-infrared fire image fusion. Owing to the growing interest in simplifying complex DL models, we have chosen the novel Adaptive Residual Fusion (ARF) method for this application. ARF leverages residual structures and adaptive selection to create highly efficient, DL-based image fusion algorithms suitable for near-infrared-visible and multi-spectral image fusion. In this study, we have chosen the SU-Net model, a U-net variant, and have evaluated the ARF approach on two prominent fire image fusion datasets, namely the airfire and fire, exhibiting high performance, efficiency, and significant error reduction, thereby ultimately leading to the development of a reliable fire detection algorithm. Early detection and treatment of depression is crucial to prevent severe consequences, making the utilization of natural language processing an effective method for identification.  In the past, researchers have employed machine learning and NLP techniques to identify depression in patient narratives, achieving moderate success.  Yet, there is a gap in ongoing research regarding the capability of users to express their depression levels in qualitative terms, encompassing three levels - mild, medium, and severe.  This study aims to address this gap, commencing with the creation of an annotated dataset of social media postings from a large population of users, who were asked to share content about their depression levels.  The dataset was then divided into three training sets and tested with multiple machine learning and NLP techniques, including word embeddings, simple text features, and neural networks, with the goal of identifying the users' depression levels.  The results of this study reveal that supervised learning methods with the use of social media data can achieve a high level of accuracy in identifying depression levels.  The qualitative nature of the depression levels also enables the machine to infer whether a user has experienced either a low or high level of severity based on their initial classification.  This study's findings have significant implications for the design of systems aimed at detecting depression, as they can now provide users with resources to help them manage their depression levels, ranging from a low of 'not severe' to an extremely severe level.  Moreover, informed system designers can utilize this understanding to craft tailored interventions aimed at assisting users in improving their depression management strategies.  In addition to these benefits, this study's results also highlight the potential for future research to combine depression levels with other user emotions to create a more comprehensive classification system.  Ultimately, this study's results provide valuable insights for researchers, designers, and practitioners to effectively detect depression levels in social media postings. In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding. Intending to address this gap, we developed a novel approach for probabilistically modeling user intent using variational autoencoders and multitask learning. By combining an attentional variational autoencoder with a multitask learning framework, our approach models user profile and goal simultaneously, leveraging a rich set of user data. We evaluated our approach with actual user data from an e-commerce platform and found that our model accurately captures underlying user characteristics. Furthermore, integrating this model into a recommender system increased the click-through rates by 15.06%, outperforming a baseline by 0.64%. The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric process. Leveraging this symmetry, we can precisely obtain the monodromy data for the equation, which is essential in different contexts like the connection problem and the Sturm-Pick problem. Uniquely, in our case, the monodromy data can be expressed in a normed form, achieving a goal that has been proposed in the literature. Building on this success, we extend our findings to a class of reducible higher-order Fuchsian equations, using a similar approach, and uncover their properties upon combining with geometric properties of the associated bidoublets in the $G_2$-Hooft matrices framework. Additionally, we reveal an intriguing connection with the CP double conic variety in the complex projective line. Moreover, the unfolding of the double confluent Heun equation serves as a precursor to the broader strategy of unfolding Fuchsian equations, which we aim to explore in future research on general higher-order Fuchsian equations. As a result of our analysis, we derive several useful identities among the monodromy data, which may be difficult to obtain through other methods. Furthermore, the found identities possess a remarkable invariance under the action of the $G_2$ group on the bidoublets, and their expression is particularly suited for automated computation via the use of algebraic methods available in computer programs like Mathematica. Importantly, our findings imply the existence of special solutions to the equation, characterized by restricted monodromy and dependence on the parameters only through their union, enabling efficient retrieval of solutions when the parameters change. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of recovering a $d$-dimensional low-rank matrix from incomplete observations, where different data blocks are subject to varying levels of noise and possibly different distributions. Building on these findings, we establish a phase transition diagram that plots the matrix recovery probability across varying levels of noise for this non-homogeneous noise model as the matrix size increases to infinity. Critical to our analysis, we develop a novel surrogate model that captures the matrix recovery process through the non-linear transformation of the matrix's eigenvectors, which changes unpredictably with the matrix order. We confirm our numerical simulations with the results of experiments and prove the model's asymptotic equivalence. This research has the potential to expand the application of phase transition studies, a widely accepted method in statistics and machine learning, to a broader range of problems. Furthermore, the introduction of new analytical tools, such as the phase transition diagram and a surrogate model, can provide a deeper understanding of low-rank matrix recovery in high-dimensional settings. The findings also shed light on the critical factors influencing matrix recovery in practice, such as sample size, matrix size, and noise heterogeneity. Ultimately, the phase transition diagram can serve as a practical performance benchmark for machine learning algorithms and statistical estimators executing on high-dimensional matrix recovery tasks. The associated R code and R Markdown files, available on GitHub, illustrate how the results were obtained and facilitate the extension of these findings to other matrix recovery problems involving linearly dependent observations. The model and analysis are also applicable to other problems involving the recovery of complex high-dimensional structures in linear systems, as demonstrated by recent extensions to the recovery of community structures in networks and the recovery of conditionally dependent signals in multi-task learning. This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally processed data, unaffected by the system-level controller. Under the assumption that the network graph adheres to a specific connectivity requirement, a decentralized controller is designed to minimize a cost function, outperforming existing distributed control methods when the network is highly segmented (many degrees of freedom). Specifically, when the network is highly connected, the proposed decentralized controller achieves the optimal cost while the distributed approach falls short. This finding confirms that a decentralized design is beneficial in highly segmented networks, a counterintuitive conclusion that challenges previous notions on the comparative merits of decentralized and distributed control designs. With this insight, a new class of distributed control methods is proposed, which in certain instances outperforms existing distributed control methods even in highly connected networks, while the proposed decentralized controller is beneficial in highly segmented networks; combining these approaches results in controllers that are co-designs. A set of numerical examples validates these analytical findings and highlights the substantial potential for improvement over existing distributed control methods for highly connected networks. Additionally, these results suggest the co-design approach offers more flexibility in achieving optimal cost values than traditional distributed and decentralized controller designs. This flexibility is further illustrated in a case study involving the coordination of swarms of drones to efficiently scan and cover a given area while maintaining communication among the drones, even in the presence of obstacles; the co-design approach enables a more effective distributed control strategy that outperforms both the decentralized and distributed control methods. This case study showcases the vast potential for applying the co-design approach in real-world networking applications. A commensurate Java code is also provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the co-design approach. The code is executed on a local server with multiple networked Java applications to simulate the coordination of 20 drones that scan and cover a given area while maintaining communication among the drones, even in the presence of obstacles; the results reveal a significant potential for improvement over existing distributed control methods for highly connected networks. A Python code is also provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the co-design approach. The code is executed on a local server with multiple networked Python applications to simulate the coordination of multiple networks that scan and cover a given area while maintaining communication among the drones, even in the presence of obstacles; the results reveal a significant potential for improvement over existing distributed control methods for highly connected networks. We've developed a COVID-19 detection framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction approach via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then combines them with temporal information from stack-based scanning. These combined features are then passed through a BERT encoder, where the dense embedding is converted into a fixed-size vector using BERT pooling. The resulting vector is then classified as COVID-19 or non-COVID-19 using a multi-layer perceptron. To further improve the model, we incorporated an ensemble method using XGBoost. The proposed framework achieved an accuracy of 85.5% and an area under the ROC curve of 0.9161 on the AICAR-COVID dataset. By leveraging the BERT pre-trained model, we overcame the limitation of limited training data. The framework outperformed existing methods, demonstrating better performance with a reduced number of parameters compared to the best previous approach. The double feature extraction strategy using 3D-CNN and BERT significantly enhanced the model's diagnostic accuracy compared to single-based methods. The proposed framework successfully identified COVID-19 cases using CT scan images with an accuracy of 85.5%, thus paving the way for clinical use. A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric of uncertainty, known as the E-value, which provides an insight into the potential impact of unobserved information. By demonstrating that large E-values indicate more robust findings resistant to changes in missing data patterns, we can interpret them as measures of statistical significance. In this study, we extend the concept of E-values to categorical outcome data with multiple levels of missingness patterns and demonstrate how this significance can be regarded as an analogue to p-values and confidence intervals. We address this challenge through a novel approach that creates a confidence interval for the E-value, offering a more comprehensive understanding of uncertainty associated with incomplete data. We perform simulations to validate our approach and showcase its application in a real-world example. This research is pioneering in providing statistical significance and confidence intervals for sensitivity analysis in the context of missing categorical outcome data. Although theoretically linked to p-values and confidence intervals, the results highlight distinct characteristics of sensitivity analysis which may lead to counterintuitive interpretations. Simulation results indicate that our approach yields reliable estimates but with smaller sample sizes required. These findings suggest that statistical conclusions based on incomplete data can be enhanced by incorporating uncertainty analysis, which may involve supplementary sensitivity analysis beyond p-values and confidence intervals. In order to increase transparency, reproducibility, and ease of use, we have provided our R code in the supplementary materials. This research is part of a larger study focusing on missing outcome data and is complemented by a related paper using Bayesian methods. In the latter, we have discovered novel Bayesian analogues of E-values, p-values, and confidence intervals. These contributions are interconnected and intended to be mutually informative. In the present paper, we have focused on frequency-based results, whereas the companion paper is based on a Bayesian perspective. One of the key differences between the two studies is the relaxed assumptions in the present paper, which is based on recent discussions indicating that frequency-based and Bayesian approaches can lead to similar conclusions when properly aligned. In addition to these findings, we have observed that the results from both papers are interdependent and may offer complementary insights and perspectives. Ultimately, we believe that the research in these two papers contributes significantly to sensitivity analysis and statistical learning.

The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Throughout 2021, we tested the "Quantum Cooler in a Box" (QCoolibax), a compact, portable cryogenic cooling system, at Fraunhofer-SU, a shared user facility in Saclay, France.
Our experiments involved two platforms: a small, 6T cryostat for small-qubit samples and a larger, 80T cryostat for bulk superconducting quantum computing systems, both of which successfully operated at 450 millikelvin using a combination of cryogenic cooling techniques and equipment.
Over a period of more than 200 operating hours in the two cryostats, the QCoolibax achieved an impressive success rate of 99.7%, demonstrating its remarkable reliability and effectiveness.
Through this study and others, we have validated the QCoolibax as a safe, efficient, and trustworthy solution for cryogenic cooling in quantum computing facilities. Furthermore, we have explored its potential for targeting even lower temperatures, potentially as low as 100 millikelvin, using advanced cryogenic techniques and equipment.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts feature unique vocabulary and orthography that reflect the grammatical structure of bygone ages. Given these complexities, automated POS annotation without biased influence from modern categories is a significant challenge. This study presents an innovative method for historical POS tagging that leverages lemmatic data from previous works and automatically generates category models. The proposed approach demonstrates notable performance in annotating text compared to previous methods, achieving effective tagging in ancient Greek, early German, and Middle English corpora. The accompanying source code is available on the GitHub platform under the username 'pos-historica'.

Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with the broader economic conditions.
This study aims to develop a machine learning-based framework for predicting the likelihood and timing of non-performing loans for individual borrowers in a specific business and economic context.
To achieve this, we assembled a comprehensive dataset of 101,951 clients and their associated financial histories, as well as macroeconomic indicators.
Using our dataset, we evaluated and compared the performance of several supervised machine learning models, including random forest, gradient boosting, and sophisticated deep learning architectures.
Our key findings reveal that factors such as age, income, loan amount, and credit history hold greater importance than other applicant characteristics when it comes to non-performing loans.
Furthermore, wez investigated the potential homoscedastic errors and non-informative priors in the probability distribution of loan-dependent variables.
Our results indicate that a well-designed deep learning model with informative priors can effectively address these issues and significantly improve forecasting accuracy for individual loan defaults.
Compared to conventional statistical methods, our approach demonstrates substantial gains in the precision of predicted timelines for non-performing loans. Additionally, we evaluated the model's generalizability by comparing the outcomes of two distinct datasets and presented evidence supporting its adaptability to different bank datasets. Based on our findings, we recommend the development of personalized risk assessment models that incorporate diverse bank data and applicant demographics. Ultimately, such models can provide more accurate and informative forecasting, serving as a valuable decision-making tool for bank professionals. The proposed model and associated code and data are publicly available for further analysis and improvement. This study contributes to the ongoing discussion regarding the application of machine learning in decision-making for individual loan assessments and non-performing loans. While the research has some limitations, it also addresses and resolves certain controversies in the field. For instance, we addressed concerns surrounding data overfitting by implementing a more efficient evaluation metric and a more accurate macroeconomic modeling approach. Our study also resolves the uncertainty surrounding the choice of machine learning model by comparing the performance of different algorithms and proposing a deep learning model with better predictive capabilities. Our work is an attempt to provide a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of individual loan defaults and non-performing loans. Our final model, informed by extensive testing, demonstrates a significant improvement over the current benchmark models and accurately captures the uncertainty associated with predicted timelines for non-performing loans. We delve into the category of shifted quasisymmetric functions to gain insights into a broader class of combinatorial interpretations for the chromatic symmetric function. By adapting techniques from the theory of divided shifted sequences, we establish a novel interpretation for the chromatic symmetric function in terms of shifted quasisymmetric functions, which reveals it as a particularly rigid instance. This approach allows us to recover known interpretations as natural consequences of a more fundamental understanding. Furthermore, it facilitates a novel interpretation in terms of the natural shifted quasisymmetric function associated with the Dyck path tableau basis, providing a combinatorial perspective on the shifted Karlovasky-Wilf conjecture. As an additional contribution, we derive a combinatorial proof of the Stanley-Chung-Wilf theorem for the chromatic symmetric function under the condition $n=2k$. The article concludes with an extension of the Dyck path tableau basis in the context of the $n=2k$ case, offering further combinatorial interpretations for the chromatic symmetric function. word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web interface. It can automatically produce a definition 
based on user-provided words and surrounding context. Furthermore, the LitMind 
Dictionary supports multilingual queries, enabling the generation of definitions 
for Chinese and English, as well as cross-language inquiries between these two 
languages. The LitMind Dictionary is accessible at https://lit-mind.d2a.info. 

This supplementary material is divided into two parts. Part 1 showcases the 
multilingual capabilities of the LitMind Dictionary by displaying queries and 
their corresponding results. Part 2 presents comprehensive evaluations and 
assessments of the dictionary's generated definitions using automatic and 
human-evaluation methods.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to a surge in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical recommendation settings. By concentrating on the nature of recommended items, a new post-hoc approach called CReAM has been developed to provide a comprehensive and objective measure of item significance. Experimental evaluations conducted using real-world datasets have demonstrated that CReAM surpasses state-of-the-art models in terms of predictive accuracy. Moreover, users who received explanations generated by CReAM reported higher levels of satisfaction, due to the system's ability to provide clear and trustworthy justifications, as compared to the baseline models. Specifically, the CReAM approach yielded notable improvements in transparency (10.0% to 23.2%) and trustworthiness (7.0% to 18.9%) when compared to the ground truth. Overall, our study highlights the importance of designing post-hoc explanations that accurately capture the underlying decision-making processes of complex models and contributes to the development of more user-centric and transparent recommender systems. As a practical implementation of the CReAM method, an open-source framework is made available to the research community to facilitate future studies in this domain. This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  Relations between the upper, lower, and convex powerspaces are established, and it is shown that, in the case of finite directed spaces, these spaces have the same structure as previous powerspaces introduced for finite posets.  The paper also defines a directed space of (finite) display maps and its corresponding powerspaces, and shows that the upper, lower, and convex powerspaces of display maps have the same structure as previous powerspaces introduced for display maps.  The paper addresses domains as a particular type of directed space with a _minimal_ set of elements and proves that, in the case of domains with a _finite_ index set (e.g., finite powerspaces of a finite domain), the upper, lower, and convex powerspaces of the domain have the same structure as previous powerspaces introduced for domains.  The paper concludes with a semantics of non-deterministic functions on directed spaces, and of dependent non-deterministic functions on one-sorted directed spaces. In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations. This method involves associating clocks with specific evaluation steps rather than functions, thereby minimizing clock annotations. Moreover, this approach facilitates the use of already available termination proof methods without additional complexity, and allows a more natural expression of termination proofs that rely on evaluation contexts. This method is effectively demonstrated through the example of small-step semantics for the $\lambda$-calculus with recursion. By applying this technique, we are able to define and prove the termination of all relevant evaluation functions using HOL's automated termination proof tool. This method, however, does impose a practical limitation in cases where a clock can be enforced by simply imposing a maximum evaluation depth, such as in the case of unguarded recursion on a non-empty list. Nevertheless, we argue that the simplicity and expressiveness gained in most cases outweighs this minor limitation. Additionally, this approach has the potential for improvement by further simplifying termination proofs. A formal description of this approach can be found in the accompanying implementation notes detailing the added abstraction and termination proofs for a small-step evaluator. Finally, this approach has been successfully validated through testing with a variety of programming languages, including call-by-need $\lambda$-terms with substitution, a simple arithmetic expression language, and even Schönfeld's $B$-terms, all of which are currently under development as part of an ongoing project. This method, however, highlights the need for further optimization techniques to effectively handle complex verification tasks. This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised emitter, in this case, a single nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre. When coupled with a localised emitter, the nanoring acts not only to enhance light absorption but also to direct light emission by operating as an optical switch. Specifically, when emitters in the system absorb resonant light, the switch enables the directed emission of this absorbed light. Our study investigates the optical spectra of the device, using a comprehensive theoretical model that incorporates both energy absorption by emitters and energy dissipation due to radiation losses. Our findings demonstrate that under resonant conditions, the device directs $77\pm2\%$ of emitter-resonant light into the far-field radiation pattern with an $8.9\pm2.2$ times higher irradiance than the non-resonant background emission. Moreover, the device functions as a low-background optical emitter with a radiative decay time of $29.4\pm0.5$ ms for NV centres resonant at $1064$ nm, resulting in an effective enhancement of emission compared to non-resonant conditions. This novel optical nanoantenna design presents a promising platform for high-efficiency optical emitters, enabling a wide range of applications in single-photon and two-photon optics. Furthermore, the device's localised emitter-based optical properties can be tailored to accommodate a broader class of emitters beyond NV centres. As a result, the device's design parameters can be adapted to accommodate emitters with varying resonance conditions, in this case, emitters resonant at $1064$ nm can be replaced with emitters resonant at $1332$ nm by adjusting the device's design. Our study lays the groundwork for the development of efficient optical emitters tailored to high-Q optical microresonators and enables the engineering of emitters that can be easily integrated into optical circuitry to form a new class of light sources with high efficiency and brightness. Consequently, the device may play a pivotal role in the development of quantum spin-based nanophotonics, enabling the detection and manipulation of unconnected NV centres at the single-spin level with high efficiency and brightness. Additionally, it's been proposed that these screenings are associated with specific structural changes rather than a universal process. Our research demonstrates that both weak and strong screenings exhibit similar temporal patterns and relate to the disappearance of specific mechanical weaknesses in the material. Consequently, these screenings appear not as different mechanisms but rather as distinct stages within the same weakening process. This study analyzes the relationship between COVID-19 news coverage in the United States and its effect on state death rates. It utilizes a time-series analysis of data from The New York Times API and finds that local news coverage initially correlated with national death rates but saw a significant decline by July 2020. Further investigation reveals that factors such as mask mandates, temperature, and demographic characteristics, including the percentage of Black and Hispanic residents, influenced the variation in state death rates and altered the correlation between news coverage and deaths over time. The study highlights how public perceptions and policy responses to the pandemic shifted as the coronavirus adapted to the warmer temperatures. It also points out an increased disparity in mortality rates among non-white populations. The researchers speculate that the initial correlation between news coverage and deaths faded as the virus became more resistant to the heat and humans acquired immunity, leading to the decreased effect of news coverage. They suggest that the increased mortality rates among non-white populations may be attributed to factors such as access to healthcare, pre-existing health conditions, and environmental factors like heat stress in communities of color. However, they emphasize that heat stress in urban areas should be a concern in its own right. Additionally, they note that the increased mortality rates among non-white populations persisted throughout the pandemic. Ultimately, they stress that the importance of factors like public awareness, healthcare access, and demographic characteristics should not be overlooked in shaping the pandemic's trajectory and its disparate effects on different populations. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities for energy, angular momentum, and kinetic energy, but preserving mass necessitates careful formulation. Spurious mass errors can lead to sub-par algorithm performance or incorrect results, often accompanied by mass oscillations. A new development framework mitigates these oscillations by enforcing mass consistency without compromising hydrodynamic stability. In combination with a thermodynamic-based viscous heat conduction method, this framework prevents spurious heat conduction phenomena. A comprehensive range of tests validates the significant reduction in mass oscillations, concurrent with improved thermal and hydrodynamic performance, in both inviscid and viscous test scenarios. This framework is compatible with a range of SPH algorithms and is adaptable to diverse physical applications. Test simulations in planetary science, astrophysics, engineering, and the medical field further demonstrate the development's robustness and potential impact. Additionally, this framework opens up new avenues for further research into SPH thermal applications. We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, presents a challenge for efficient learning, particularly when dealing with large datasets. To address this limitation, we present a new algorithm that leverages the creation of synthetic experience to boost data efficiency. The policy cloning problem is reformulated as a neural radial flow optimization task and solved using a gradient-based optimization algorithm. This approach condenses a large dataset into a reduced, representative subset and accelerates the learning process significantly. Experimental results demonstrate our algorithm's ability to outperform existing methods, achieving substantial gains in efficiency, particularly with limited data availability. We showcase the effectiveness of our algorithm by successfully reducing the time required for learning across multiple challenging domain-specific tasks, such as data-efficient visual navigation in 3D environments and learning complex manipulation skills from expert demonstrations. Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop, thereby meeting the necessary phase condition.
Using a compact optical cavity and a 2-level maser system, we successfully leverage the sensitivity of the resonant detection to minuscule changes in the cavity's optical refractive index, detecting an optical spin maser noise level of 1 nW/rms.
This level of sensitivity allows us to sense extremely small changes in the cavity, including microscopic additions such as individual silicon nanoparticles. 
As a demonstration of the technology's capabilities, we successfully detected a silicon nanoparticle with a diameter of about 20 nm added to the cavity. 
This detection capability was possible due to the technology's extremely high dynamic range, about 1000 times more sensitive than other similar detection technologies, and the ability to distinguish the background magnetic field without any external reference. 
As a result of the technology's small size, low cost, and high sensitivity, we predict that these self-oscillating atomic magnetometers will play a major role in future advancements in optical cavities and maser technology.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, they need to create an accurate 3D map while also localizing themselves on that map. Existing research often relies on complete information, but in real-world scenarios, this isn't always the case, and robots have to navigate through uncertainty, taking actions without full information about their environment. We propose an efficient new method that utilizes a map to inform decision-making even when the 3D environment is invisible. This method uses the predicted map to localize itself by generating a probability distribution of possible poses and then selecting the one that aligns best with the estimated map. To test this approach, we integrated it into a existing system for 3D map-based navigation in unknown environments and evaluated its performance through simulations on challenging "Seeing is Believing" tasks. Our results show that this method outperforms previous baselines by efficiently constructing an accurate 3D map while also accurately localizing itself within that map. This new approach represents a significant improvement in map-based navigation in uncertainty, achieving an average localization error of 0.16m, 0.12m, and 0.10m in test scenarios with increasing levels of obscurability. This method also efficiently processes sensor data, taking only 0.03s to 0.06s in total, and map construction in the test scenario takes around 30s. These results show that this method outperforms previous approaches by a factor of 2.8 and 6.1. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. A video of this method can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KQw6sK9L6gA.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively used in both clinical settings and industrial applications that require the internal composition of objects. Most CT systems utilize X-ray sources that emit a multi-energy spectrum, leading to beam hardening, flux fluctuations, and scatter radiation, which cause additional distortions in reconstructed images. In CT technology, these distortions can be minimized or eliminated through the implementation of various correction techniques, such as calibration-based approaches, iterative algorithms, and filtered back-projection methods with beam hardening correction. This article focuses on the development of a novel filtered back-projection framework that automatically corrects for the effects of polyenergetic X-ray sources, either by directly using measured attenuation measurements or estimated projections, to approximate the monochromatic CT image. It is demonstrated that this new framework produces high-quality reconstructions that match the output of iterative reconstruction algorithms while significantly reducing their computational requirements. Experimental results confirm that this new technique achieves satisfactory accuracy with minimal computational effort. The proposed framework is expected to contribute to the development of polyenergetic CT technology, making it more suitable for a wider range of applications. The numerous advancements in extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) have significantly improved our understanding of diseases and healthcare treatments. Although machine learning models have shown great potential in utilizing EHR data, there is a major drawback to this approach - datasets are often compiled from diverse sources with varying data formats, rendering it challenging to leverage the power of these models effectively. To address this limitation, this research introduces the Hospital Information Analytics System (HIAS), a cloud-based platform capable of integrating and standardizing data from different hospitals, converting raw data into unified feature sets suitable for machine learning models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by using a combined dataset from multiple hospitals to train a predictive model that achieves an impressive 88% accuracy in identifying patients at risk of certain conditions. By offering a cloud-deployed platform, healthcare institutions can benefit from a standardized approach to utilizing EHR data for machine learning tasks. Our study showcases the HIAS platform's ability to improve predictive diagnosis accuracy through a case study. Additionally, this research has significant implications for future studies utilizing machine learning models to extract valuable insights from diverse healthcare datasets. We believe that raw data across these studies can be integrated and re-labeled to enable more robust machine learning-based tasks, ultimately leading to better healthcare outcomes. Furthermore, a community-driven resource is being established to support the development of data standardization tools, data merging algorithms, and feature engineering techniques, aiming to address the major drawback of fragmented healthcare datasets in the research field. With sufficient resources and community support, the goal is to enable researchers to leverage the power of large-scale datasets effectively, ultimately leading to better healthcare outcomes. To this end, a comprehensive software package, including code for data standardization and feature engineering, as well as the HIAS platform, is being made available on public repositories, namely GitHub and DBCP. We believe that a collaborative effort among researchers, developers, and clinicians is crucial in addressing the complex challenge of utilizing machine learning models to improve patient care. By promoting community-driven development and knowledge sharing, we can significantly accelerate advancements in this critical area and pave the way for more effective use of machine learning models to improve patient care. The research presented in this paper is a crucial step in addressing this challenge, laying the groundwork for future studies that can leverage the power of large-scale datasets effectively. We believe that a collaborative, knowledge-sharing community is essential in addressing this complex challenge, and we look forward to continued development in this area. agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have several limitations, particularly 
regarding their privacy implications. This research aims to develop a solution 
by adapting Federated Learning for the satellite imaging domain. It addresses 
three key challenges: creating simulated satellite image datasets for FL training; 
evaluating the effectiveness of FL training versus traditional training; and

data. The results demonstrate that FL can produce models of comparable quality to 
those trained centrally, while the application of simulated data significantly 
enhances the models' ability to identify objects in images without exposing the 
original data to potential security threats. This research offers a promising 
approach for the satellite imaging sector to balance data analysis, computation, 
privacy, and knowledge updates in a decentralized environment. The accompanying

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a challenging task that becomes increasingly difficult due to varying lesion appearance and context. Current deep learning techniques have shown promise, however they can be hindered by label scarcity due to the high editing requirements for training data. Since manual labeling is time-consuming and labor-intensive, generating more data through virtual labeling is essential. But conventional virtual labeling methods often introduce errors by generating unrealistic lesions, leading to model distortion. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel virtual labeling method based on CycleGAN that can automatically synthesize high-quality training data without manual intervention. Our method not only removes the need for manual editing but also preserves the statistical integrity of the training set. In our experiments, we have found that using the new CycleGAN virtual labeling approach leads to significantly better lesion segmentation performance compared to conventional virtual labeling techniques, and also improves the segmentation accuracy when augmented with a small amount of manually labeled data. With proper augmentation, our method can generate an unlimited amount of synthetic data for improving MS lesion segmentation accuracy. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  The mass discrepancy may also be linked to the varying levels of accretion rates among the cores in question, as determined by their calculated total column densities and the rates of molecular outflows.  In particular, cores with higher mass addition are found to possess greater outflow rates as well as higher infrared emission.  The measured mass addition among the cores, along with the rates of molecular outflows, can be used to estimate the cores' surrounding ambient mass accretion rates.  In this context, cores with higher mass addition are found to possess lower accretion rates at their outer boundaries, with estimated values of approximately $3 \times 10^{-7}~\mathrm{M_{\odot}~yr^{-1}}$.  In the process of forming a protostar, a significant increase in mass accretion occurs, specifically from the previously established core mass of $\sim 10~M_{\odot}$. The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can be identified by distinct characteristics in the gravitational wave signal they would emit upon merging with other black holes. We analyzed data from a recent gravitational wave experiment and found no evidence of this signal, setting limits on the mass range in which primordial black holes would exist. Our study used distinct signals generated by different types of black holes and considered various possible sources of error, taking into into account varying levels of uncertainty. We found that certain of these uncertainties would allow for the possibility of primordial black holes existing in the range of masses from approximately 14 to 42 times that of the sun. However, the likelihood of this existing range being consistent with a natural fluctuation in the universe was assessed and found to be relatively small. Additionally, we found that there is only a minimal probability that primordial black holes represent the bulk of dark matter in the universe. While we ruled out certain possibilities for the mass of these black holes, we found that there is a small chance that a certain range of these black holes exist and could potentially account for a significant portion of dark matter in certain scenarios.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to large pre-trained language models to accommodate new tasks, which typically requires significant adjustments to their parameters. Currently available solutions, such as few-shot and adapter-based approaches, have notable limitations: the former needs an extensive number of examples to train the adapter, which may not be feasible to obtain, and the latter increases computational overhead due to the need to multiply the embedding dimensions. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new technique, the single-head adapter, which offers an attractive middle ground. It allows the model to focus on specific features of the input by simply shifting the balance within the default multi-head distribution established during pre-training. Our single-head adapter is an innovative variation of the traditional adapter that efficiently tunes the attention between different input sequences. It's an essential component of our PEFSE framework, which enables efficient tuning by assigning a unique adapter to each token based on the positional encoding. By positioning the adapter according to the positional encoding, the adapter is given the opportunity to capture the unique characteristics of the input sequence, which are determined by the positional encoding. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing datasets, which reveals a models' inability to accurately answer many questions involving certain types of negation. Our analysis identifies areas for improvement and suggests customizing datasets to enhance NLP capabilities. Additionally, we discuss how this research contributes to a more nuanced understanding of NLP systems. Our code and data are available online.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source words, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words, which are themselves influenced by past predictions, thereby introducing historical dependency issues. Building on this insight, this paper proposes a novel structure that integrates the attention model with a target word error correction component, incorporating a source sentence mask, along with a target word mask that evolves incrementally during prediction, reflecting the increasing probability of target word errors as generation progresses.
